items.title: Lodos: A Lightweight Simulator Designed for Contact-Rich Interactions with Detailed Meshes
items.content: arXiv:2611.08872v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In recent years, massively parallelized rigid-body simulation has played a central role in robotics research, enabling rapid progress in areas such as reinforcement learning, stochastic optimal control, and randomized smoothing-based trajectory optimization. Particularly in contact-rich settings, the scalability of such simulations in large part depends on well-optimized representations of collision geometry, often requiring a coarse approximation of the underlying surfaces using primitives such as spheres, capsules, cylinders, and boxes. Whenever the complexity of the surfaces or the precision demands of the application render such approximations insufficient, it is instead necessary to employ mesh-mesh collisions, which impose a significant reduction in throughput. This paper proposes a simulation framework designed from scratch to address this bottleneck, with novel routines for broadphase and narrowphase collision detection as well as the subsequent contact dynamics computation. As experimentally validated, the framework matches existing well-established simulators in terms of physical faithfulness, and can achieve approximately an order of magnitude higher throughput in the detailed mesh-mesh collision setting that it specializes in. The source code is available at https://github.com/martius-lab/lodos.
items.author: Onur Beker, Andreas Ren\'e Geist, Georg Martius
items.summary: Lodos is a massively parallel rigid-body simulator focused on contact-rich interactions using detailed mesh-mesh collisions rather than coarse primitive approximations, supporting RL, stochastic optimal control, and trajectory optimization research. It is the predecessor system that Lodos-v2 improves upon.
items.reasoning: Mesh-level collision fidelity in parallel simulation fills a real gap, since most fast simulators rely on primitive geometry. The core novelty, however, is largely superseded by its companion paper Lodos-v2, and the abstract frames it as foundational infrastructure rather than a conceptual breakthrough.

items.title: Extended Model-Based Learned Inertial Odometry
items.content: arXiv:2611.09584v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Inertial odometry is a compelling approach to state estimation for agile quadrotor flight due to its affordability, low weight, and robustness to perceptual degradation. However, relying only on integrated inertial measurements is impractical, as sensor errors and time-varying biases lead to significant pose drift. Although recent advances have enabled inertial odometry for drone racing, existing approaches show limited generalization to trajectories not seen during training. This work improves generalization by adopting a body-frame representation and incorporating body-frame torque dynamics into the learning pipeline. The learned model predicts short-horizon relative displacements, which are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for quadrotor pose estimation on unseen trajectories. An additional evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets, with whole trajectory shapes held out of training, confirms a lower velocity error on every held-out set and shows that the torque input is most informative when it is derived from the rotor signals. Code, data pipeline and trained models are publicly available.

items.title: What do LLMs Really Learn About Model Weights? A Stratification Approach to Examine Weight Space Programming
items.content:
# TLDR

I attempted to replicate “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” by Takehi et al (2026) with stratification on two reasoning models, GPT 6 Astra and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash. The task for the LLMs is to identify the game a ML model is trained for giving the weight of the model (using exact same prompt and weight defined by Takehi).

Although both of these models do well on the surface (4/4 correct for Astra and 3/4 correct for Flash), the stratification approach exposes the difference in mechanism between these two models in approaching the problem. The experiment result shows that Flash depends a lot on channel label for the answer (while Astra's performance does not degrade when channel label does not present). Additionally, Astra is able to identify the game with good accuracy using only the first layer of weight or as few as 1000 weight values selected at random out of 17253 weight values (Flash's performance degrade substantially on these).

So Astra survives this first round of stratification tests just for now. Comparing the results between Astra and Flash, it is obvious that Flash is relying heavily on prompt metadata instead of reading the weights.

# Background

On November 2 an article “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming” was published by Takehi et al (2026). The article is cleanly written and one of the claims is that by looking at model weights, GPT 6 Astra can tell what the model is trained to do. The article reports that Astra is able to name the game a ML model is trained for in four different cases (Breakout, Pong, Pac-man, Freeway) directly through the weight of the model without use of external tools.

If LLMs do have capability to read model weights and identify what it is trained to do, this would have huge implications in the fields of interpretability and weight auditing without evaluation as suggested by the article by Takehi et al (2026)....
items.author: CCaptainX
items.summary: The author replicates Takehi et al's 2026 weight-space programming result with two reasoning models, GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, asking them to identify a trained model's task from its weights, then applies stratification tests (removing channel labels, using only the first layer, or small random weight subsets) to distinguish genuine weight-reading from metadata shortcuts. Astra's performance survives stratification while Flash's degrades sharply, suggesting Flash relies on prompt metadata.
items.reasoning: Original, well-designed empirical work probing whether LLMs genuinely interpret neural network weights, with a stratification methodology that usefully separates mechanism from surface accuracy on frontier models. The single-author, blog-format setting and small task set limit confidence, but the approach is novel and relevant to model introspection and capability evaluation.

items.title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference
items.content: arXiv:2611.08741v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.
items.author: Alexander Kastius
items.summary: AlterNet combines Mixture-of-Experts with shallow experts and a dynamic-depth mechanism using learned halting, letting a model decide how much compute each forward pass needs and scale compute down after training without retraining. It introduces sequence-level depth routing, a depth encoding for tracking progress, and regularization to support elastic inference.

We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.

items.title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.09232v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.

The integration and interactive explainability angle is useful, but the underlying techniques are standard, limiting methodological novelty.

items.title: Relic and Gumi: Governing Memory, Safety, and Continuity in Diegetic Relational Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.08504v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say.   We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system.   We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.

items.title: FoleyForge: Free-form, Controllable, Rectified-flow Editing of Sound Effects
items.content: arXiv:2611.08695v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We present FoleyForge, a generative model for instruction-based editing of sound effects. Given an input clip and a free-form instruction describing the desired change, it applies the edit while preserving the input's identity. A single model handles semantic, stylistic, and DSP-like changes. We introduce a data pipeline that guides an audio language model to author both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits, thus addressing the lack of publicly available audio editing data. Such data is then used to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generation model, which we extend to expose attribute controls for loudness change, edit strength, and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable via classifier-free guidance, yielding a more expressive editing model. FoleyForge achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.

items.title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
items.content: arXiv:2611.09274v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable performance based on parametric knowledge, i.e., their ability to recall facts and associations internalized in a model's weights. However, studying this capability on established multi-hop benchmarks may be complicated by benchmark contamination, as many of these benchmarks have been publicly available long enough to plausibly appear in modern pretraining corpora. As a result, correct answers under missing evidence may reflect either general parametric knowledge or memorization of benchmark-specific instances. To study how models use internal knowledge when retrieval evidence is incomplete, we introduce FondueQA, in which every required multi-hop fact is uniquely localized to a designated evidence document. This enables controlled document-level evidence ablations to study parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval. Our empirical evaluation reveals that parametric compensation strongly depends on both entity popularity and the structural role of missing evidence. Generally, models compensate more successfully for facts involving popular entities. On FondueQA, we show that bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document itself. Moreover, models may recall a missing fact in isolation but fail to use it under partial evidence, particularly when the context contains plausible competing entities, which can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.
items.author: Laurin Schmid, Suman Navaratnarajah, Koel Dutta Chowdhury, Steffen Eger, Josif Grabocka, Christian Frey
items.summary: Introduces FondueQA, a multi-hop QA benchmark where each required fact is uniquely localized to designated evidence, enabling controlled study of how models compensate for incomplete retrieval with parametric knowledge while controlling for benchmark contamination and memorization. It distinguishes genuine parametric knowledge from memorized benchmark instances.
items.reasoning: Well-designed benchmark addressing the increasingly important dual problems of contamination and the interaction between retrieval and parametric knowledge. Valuable for evaluation methodology, though multi-hop QA benchmarks are numerous and long-term adoption is uncertain.

items.title: Not All Entropy Is Equal: Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
items.content: arXiv:2611.09448v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Policy entropy is widely used to diagnose exploration and collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yet its magnitude does not consistently track reasoning performance across optimization objectives. We argue that this ambiguity arises because global token entropy conflates uncertainty in successful and failed trajectories, diversity across correct solution strategies, and variation among realizations of the same strategy. We introduce \textbf{Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation (RCEA)}, a hierarchical diagnostic framework that separates complete-trajectory entropy from average token entropy, conditions uncertainty on verifier outcome and process validity, measures correct-solution-mode retention, and connects these population-level quantities to local covariance-driven updates. In controlled sweeps over six RLVR objectives at two model scales, entropy trajectories do not induce a stable ordering of reasoning accuracy. Token entropy is higher for verifier-failed than successful trajectories under both broad separately aggregated estimates and a common-question paired analysis, whose confidence intervals exclude equality at 10 of 12 displayed endpoints. A local covariance approximation predicts the direction of adjacent-checkpoint entropy change in 95.5\% of nonfailed transitions; a reward-stratified endpoint proxy further shows that positive chosen-token covariance is more tail-concentrated within failed prefixes. Every reportable trained endpoint exhibits some contraction in independently audited correct-solution-mode breadth, whose positive association with large-\(k\) coverage remains exploratory. These results show that entropy collapse should be diagnosed by which uncertainty is removed, rather than by global entropy alone.
items.author: Song Yu, Li Li, Zhenming Wu
items.summary: This paper argues that global token entropy is an ambiguous diagnostic for RLVR because it conflates uncertainty in successful versus failed trajectories, diversity across correct strategies, and variation among realizations of one strategy. It introduces Reward-Conditioned Entropy Allocation (RCEA), a hierarchical diagnostic framework that separates trajectory from token entropy and conditions uncertainty on verifier outcomes. This provides sharper tools for understanding exploration and collapse in reasoning RL.
items.reasoning: Refines a widely used but poorly understood diagnostic in the very active RLVR area; conceptual contribution is useful for the community, though it is an analytical/diagnostic framework rather than a new algorithm.

items.title: V-STORM: A Structure-Aware Grounded Chain of Thought Dataset for Faithful and Fine-Grained Spatio-Temporal Video Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.09511v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.

items.summary: V-STORM presents a framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives grounded chains of thought from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to verifiable spatio-temporal evidence. This provides granular, verifiable supervision for fine-grained video reasoning where multimodal LLMs currently struggle with when-and-where grounding. As a dataset and pipeline contribution it could become a useful resource for training and evaluating video reasoning models.

items.title: MEDALLION: Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON
items.content: arXiv:2611.08767v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Dimensionality reduction is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data and guide scientific discovery, yet interpreting which original features contribute to low-dimensional representations remains challenging, particularly for black-box methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. We introduce \textbf{MEDALLION} (Manifold Embedding Distillation and Attributions for Low-dimensional Latent InterpretatiON), a novel framework for interpreting low-dimensional embeddings through knowledge distillation and neural feature attribution. MEDALLION distills any given embedding with a neural encoder which we explain via a broad range of existing neural feature attribution methods. Through experiments on MNIST and applications in single-cell transcriptomics, we show MEDALLION provides informative feature attributions that cast additional insights into the underlying embedding and compare its performance with existing interpretability approaches.

items.summary: MEDALLION interprets black-box dimensionality reduction embeddings such as t-SNE and UMAP by distilling them into a neural encoder and applying feature attribution methods to identify which original features drive low-dimensional structure. Demonstrations on MNIST and single-cell transcriptomics show practical value for scientific discovery workflows.
items.reasoning: Addresses a real, widespread gap — interpreting UMAP/t-SNE embeddings — with a general, model-agnostic framework and a compelling scientific application in genomics; novelty is moderate since it composes existing distillation and attribution techniques.

items.title: StreamTab: Training-Free Temporal Link Prediction with Tabular Foundation Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.09052v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Temporal link prediction uses past interactions to predict whether two nodes will interact in the future. Temporal graph neural networks achieve strong results on this task, but they are trained separately for each graph. How a model should use interaction history also depends on the candidates it is compared with. A past interaction can distinguish a recurring link from a random pair that has never interacted, but when the negative candidates have also interacted before, other signals are needed. We propose StreamTab, a training-free framework built on a frozen tabular foundation model pretrained only on synthetic tables. StreamTab describes each candidate pair by statistics of its past interactions and shows the model recent observed interactions and sampled negative pairs as labeled examples, from which the model scores new candidates. Its central design, regime conditioning, samples the negative examples according to how the candidates are sampled, so the examples show the distinction the model must make. As new interactions arrive, StreamTab updates the statistics and refreshes the examples while the model parameters stay fixed. On thirteen datasets against 21 temporal graph baselines, StreamTab achieves the highest average precision on twelve datasets under historical sampling and eleven under inductive sampling, and ranks first or stays within one point of the best on seven datasets under random sampling. With the same features and model, regime conditioning raises average precision over examples with random negatives by a median of 12.6 points under historical sampling.

It represents candidate node pairs via statistics of past interactions and in-context recent observations, avoiding per-graph training required by temporal GNNs. This demonstrates that tabular foundation models can transfer to temporal graph tasks without fine-tuning.

items.title: The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power
items.content: arXiv:2611.09815v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Uncertainty bands on wind forecasts help inform reserve sizing and commitments, but often fail to deliver their stated coverage. We apply conformal prediction to native bands to see what it adds and what it costs, comparing six forecasters, from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain (GB) under operational conditions. We show that calibration repairs empirical marginal coverage with little or no Winkler Score penalty, but this apparent success conceals under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating by forecast wind regime turns marginal coverage into regime-level coverage, cutting day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40% relative to pooled calibration while narrowing bands overall.

items.summary: Applies conformal prediction to native wind-power forecast uncertainty bands at two Great Britain wind farms, comparing six forecasters from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model. It shows calibration repairs marginal coverage cheaply but masks under-coverage in high winds, and regime-wise calibration cuts day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40 percent.
items.reasoning: A well-grounded operational study with practical value for renewable energy forecasting and a genuinely useful finding about the limits of pooled conformal calibration. Scope is limited to two wind farms, which caps generalizability.

items.title: Finite-sample Calibration Guarantees for Binary Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.09120v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Machine learning based segmentation models are frequently miscalibrated, producing for each pixel a label prediction whose associated confidence does not accurately reflect the true underlying probability. This limitation is particularly critical in high-stakes applications such as medical image segmentation. Although several calibration methods have been proposed, only a small subset of them provides theoretical guarantees on the calibration error, i.e., they do not typically ensure that, with high probability, the model exhibits a low calibration error. In this work, we develop a post-hoc calibration method for which formal calibration guarantees can be established. To achieve this, we derive from standard concentration inequalities an improved theoretical bound that explicitly accounts for the spatial dependence inherent in binary segmentation outputs. We empirically demonstrate that the proposed calibrator satisfies the derived guarantee and outperforms existing post-hoc calibration approaches.

items.title: MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition
items.content: arXiv:2611.09090v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation relies heavily on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking from multilingual collections, which are vulnerable to cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead. In this paper, we explore retriever-free multilingual search, where the model directly interacts with raw corpora through executable shell commands. This paradigm shifts the bottleneck to multilingual search action generation, where exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision provides limited guidance for multi-turn search. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a multilingual search agent in direct corpus interaction (DCI) with reinforcement learning (RL). MARS introduces corpus-native entity grounding to recover reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, mitigating failure to retrieve evidence. Meanwhile, we present a redundancy-aware search reward to encourage concise and effective search trajectories, addressing training collapse in RL of multilingual scenarios. Experiments show that \ours~consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines, while demonstrating robust cross-lingual generalization and substantially reducing redundant corpus interactions.

items.title: On Seeding Watermarks to Detect Verbatim LLM Copy-Paste Responses
items.content: arXiv:2605.16336v2 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made fluent essay writing, code drafting, and quiz answering instantly available to students at every level, from secondary school through graduate study. Many educators do not object to LLM use \emph{per~se}; what they need to detect is the case in which a student pastes the assignment prompt into a chatbot and submits the model's reply verbatim, without engaging with the work. Existing post-hoc AI-text detectors remain unreliable and have been shown to penalise non-native English writers, while output-side watermarks require cooperation from the model provider. We propose an alternative that the educator controls directly: an input-side watermark in which an invisible instruction is embedded inside the visible assignment prompt itself. An LLM that ingests the prompt verbatim quietly reads the hidden instruction and writes a tell-tale signature into its reply, exposing the copy-and-paste pathway specifically. We describe SteganoPrompt, a single-page, zero-dependency web tool that encodes an arbitrary printable-ASCII payload into the deprecated Unicode Tags block (\texttt{U+E0000}--\texttt{U+E007F}). The encoded string is visually identical to the original, survives common copy-paste channels (Word, Google Docs, PDF, Markdown, Slack, e-mail, the major learning-management systems), and is tokenized as ordinary text by most frontier models. We evaluate compliance across eight LLM families and a representative set of educational content channels. To keep deployment transparent, disclosure is built into the tool itself: every encoded brief also carries a brief, always-on academic-integrity reminder for the student, and we set out concrete guidance recommending for its disclosed, ethical use in the classroom. The tool is released under the MIT licence at https://ezharjan.github.io/SteganoPrompt/.

items.title: MetricPose: Flexible 3D Human Pose Estimation with Depth and Geometric Cues
items.content: arXiv:2611.08954v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper, we present a 3D human pose estimator that predicts metrically accurate human joint positions in the camera coordinate frame. This task requires recovering the configuration of the body joints, scale, and metric camera-local placement. In monocular images, body size and camera distance are coupled through perspective projection and therefore cannot be determined uniquely from image alone. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining three complementary sources of information: learned RGB priors, direct depth measurements, and geometric constraints (e.g., ground contact) from the environment. We extend a pretrained full-body estimator with optional metric depth and geometry-processing modules that improve camera-distance estimation and depth-guided body refinement while preserving RGB-only operation. The resulting unified model supports RGB, RGB-Ground, and RGB-D using shared learned parameters. Unlike pelvis-relative error, camera-local error also measures placement relative to the camera. Compared with the existing foundation model SAM 3D Body, our methods with RGB, RGB-Ground, and RGB-D modes reduce camera-local joint-position error by 12.16%, 31.00% and 54.61% respectively.

items.title: Keyline Detection with YOLO: Runway Perception for Vision-Based Aircraft Landing
items.content: arXiv:2611.09316v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Modern object detectors can predict keypoints as per-object geometric features, but keypoints are inherently vulnerable to occlusion and truncation. Object edges can provide complementary information, often remaining observable even when partially occluded or when their defining endpoints leave the field of view. We therefore introduce object keyline detection, the task of predicting a fixed, semantically ordered set of infinite lines per object instance. Unlike the outputs of general line-segment detectors, each keyline is associated with an object instance and identified by a semantic index, providing a line-level analog of keypoints. To solve this task, we extend YOLO with keyline prediction parameterized in continuous Hesse-normal form $[\rho,\cos\theta,\sin\theta]$, and introduce Object Keyline Similarity (OKLS), which serves as an evaluation metric, target assignment signal, and regression loss. We instantiate this formulation on runway perception in vision-based landing, a motivating example containing semantic linear features that remain partially observable throughout the approach. Experiments show that our representation achieves the highest detection accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations, and keylines integrate directly into standard YOLO heads as additional output channels without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.

items.title: Seeing What Matters: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.09794v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? Spatial-reasoning benchmarks evaluate whether a model can describe a scene, but manipulation needs something more specific: the ability to acquire the particular evidence that makes the current command executable. A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Matters, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Across three domains--coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance--the benchmark provides 860 frozen evaluation cases; expanding across methods, budgets, and inference repeats yields more than 115,000 evaluator episodes under two protocols: closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization. Each case pairs a set of candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, so the benchmark directly measures whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations its command actually needs. We also provide a diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, this pipeline reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; ablating the functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero. Seven vision-language models, evaluated on the same cases, reach only 26-43%. Replacing the reference pipeline's coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores preserves 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling the visual scores collapses it to 15%/11%, confirming that the result depends on image content. These gaps suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated not by scene-level completeness, but by whether it acquires the evidence the current command requires.

items.summary: This benchmark evaluates whether embodied agents acquire the specific visual evidence needed to execute a manipulation command, rather than merely describing scenes, across three simulated tabletop domains with 860 frozen evaluation cases and over 115,000 evaluator episodes. It formalizes task-conditioned actionable spatial belief as a distinct capability from generic spatial reasoning.
items.reasoning: Conceptually sharp reframing of spatial benchmarks around task-conditioned evidence gathering for manipulation; simulation-only scope and modest author visibility temper the score.

items.title: HOC2R: Hand-Object Contact Trajectories for Human-to-Robot Motion Transfer
items.content: arXiv:2611.08920v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.

items.title: Locating Contact on Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots From Tendon Measurements Alone via Constrained Moving Horizon Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2611.09877v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Without contact, the MHE offered no advantage over the EKF, which confirms that its benefit comes from the contact constraints. This report extends a letter submitted to IEEE Control Systems Letters with complete proofs and additional experiments.

It then shows that with known obstacle geometry, non-penetration and complementarity conditions restore local identifiability, and presents a real-time constrained moving horizon estimator that exploits these constraints to locate contact.

Its scope is fairly narrow and specialized to continuum robots with known obstacle geometry, limiting broad impact, but methodological rigor is high.

items.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
items.content: arXiv:2611.08644v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge.   We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query.   Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.

However, the evaluation environment is deterministic and mocked, leaving open questions about real-world generalization; the system is also product-adjacent rather than a fundamental research advance.

items.title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.08855v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. items.title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
items.content: arXiv:2611.09263v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.

items.title: Challenges, Opportunities, and Misconceptions in Neurosymbolic AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.09356v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We examine opportunities for neurosymbolic AI alongside increasingly powerful neural models, particularly with regards to efficiency, safety and interpretability. We identify two major challenges: ensuring semantic alignment between neural and symbolic components, and managing the computational cost of symbolic inference and learning. We discuss representative methodological approaches to these challenges and address several common misconceptions concerning differentiability, independence assumptions, and scalability. This paper synthesizes perspectives developed through discussions in the Neurosymbolic Programming and Reasoning (NPR) working group at the 2026 CNRS workshop Neurosymbolic Methods and Their Applications in Data Science, rather than providing an exhaustive survey.

items.title: Atik: A Shared-Mesh Transformer Accelerator for RISC-V
items.content: arXiv:2611.09522v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Transformer inference repeatedly invokes dense matrix multiplication and attention, including its data-dependent softmax normalization. We present Atik, an open-source RoCC accelerator for RocketChip that executes matrix multiplication and dense attention through one shared fixed-point MAC mesh. Atik accepts and returns BF16 tensors, uses a streaming online-softmax schedule that never materializes the full score matrix, and is invoked through a small descriptor-based ABI. We evaluate three meshes cycle-by-cycle on FireSim and report standalone Sky130 physical-design area. Across 137 logged FireSim test records, all tests pass their benchmark tolerance with zero reported output mismatches. Relative to the same scalar Rocket BF16 reference, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul speedup and 225.8x peak attention speedup. Hybrid projections for the single-layer workload-derived C models, using directly measured accelerator-kernel cycles, give aggregate speedups of 44.2x, 77.1x, and 32.3x for ViT, TinyBERT, and GPT-2 prefill, respectively; these are not full-model hardware replays.

items.title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
items.content: arXiv:2611.09730v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.

items.title: VoluCompose: Constructing Compact Volumetric Visual Representations for Medical Image Understanding
items.content: arXiv:2611.08649v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.

items.title: Training-Free Active Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.09084v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/ACTOR.

The method is training-free, sidestepping the restriction that models must repair their own uncertain predictions without external evidence.
items.reasoning: Well-motivated problem formulation bridging active learning and test-time adaptation for VLMs, with practical deployment relevance given explicit labeling budgets. Training-free design adds practical value, though the contribution is incremental within a rapidly moving TTA literature.

items.title: AudioSphere: Towards Self-Supervised Spatial Audio Representation Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.09275v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent audio embedding models learn representations that transfer across clip- and frame-level tasks, yet they operate almost exclusively on single-channel signals and are blind to spatial structure. Spatial audio models capture that structure but rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, yielding embeddings unsuitable for frame-level tasks like sound event detection and localization (SELD). We argue this dichotomy is not fundamental: patch-level spatial self-supervision can jointly learn acoustic and spatial features at both temporal granularities. We introduce AudioSphere, a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that reconstructs both spectral content and directional cues via a joint spatiotemporal masking strategy that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors. AudioSphere supports frame-level predictions while producing strong clip-level representations via aggregation. Alongside the model, we release RealSELD, a standardized benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world multi-channel SELD. AudioSphere enables, for the first time, SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone, while matching or exceeding prior self-supervised audio embedding models on clip-level classification tasks spanning environmental sound, speech, and music, and on frame-level sound event detection. All code and data are available at https://github.com/labhamlet/AudioSphere and https://huggingface.co/labhamlet.

It bridges the gap between audio embedding models blind to spatial structure and spatial audio models unsuited to frame-level tasks like sound event detection and localization.

items.title: HiMEM: Hippocampus-Inspired Memory Consolidation, Pruning, and Composition for Vision-Language-Action Models in 3D Scenes
items.content: arXiv:2611.09355v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Memory plays a crucial role in long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models operating in complex 3D scenes. However, existing VLA memory mechanisms suffer from memory noise, particularly in complex 3D scenes, as stored episodic memories contain extensive redundant details about scene layouts, object configurations, and robot-specific states, which obscure generalizable manipulation principles and hinder cross-task transfer. To address this challenge, we first introduce a hippocampus-inspired memory consolidation mechanism that synthesizes extensive episodic experiences into a compact set of essential semantic memories, enabling VLA models to derive generalizable principles from practical experience. Second, we propose an episodic memory pruning mechanism that removes redundant episodic memories whose contents are captured by consolidated semantic memories, thereby increasing effective memory capacity and improving long-horizon task execution. Finally, to handle complex task scenarios, we develop a flexible memory composition mechanism that jointly leverages multiple episodic and semantic memories to enhance cross-scenario generalization. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus demonstrate the effectiveness of HiMEM across different VLA backbones, improving the average success rate of pi_0 from 91.88% to 98.20% on LIBERO.

This enables better long-horizon task execution and cross-task generalization by pruning redundant scene- and robot-specific details. The bio-inspired framing applied to robot memory systems is a creative contribution to embodied AI.

items.title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.09770v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.
items.author: Lingyun Song, Ziyao Chen, Kang Pan, Xiaolin Han, Yifei Zhang, Xiaoqi Wang, Yudai Pan, Xuequn Shang
items.summary: ROSE is a framework for lifelong knowledge editing in multimodal LLMs that restricts sequential edits to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces and uses a dynamically computed risk mask to protect specific factual parameters. This targets the twin problems of locality erosion and catastrophic forgetting in continual model updating. It matters because keeping deployed multimodal models factually current without degrading capabilities is a pressing practical need.
items.reasoning: Solid methodological contribution to an active subfield (knowledge editing), combining orthogonal-subspace and risk-mask ideas; incremental relative to prior editing work and from an academic group, but addresses a real problem in MLLMs specifically.

ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.

items.title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
items.content: arXiv:2611.08551v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.

items.title: Global Solar Siting from Geospatial Embeddings
items.content: arXiv:2611.08831v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Global solar photovoltaic (PV) capacity is rapidly growing, helping decrease our emissions and dependence on fossil fuels. However, optimally siting a solar plant remains challenging, requiring anticipation of geographical, urban, and infrastructure needs. Current methods rely on multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) using hand-picked geophysical layers and solar-resource products, however these strategies are not geographically transferable and do not capture the practical requirements of solar sites. We use geospatial embeddings, dense vectors representing geophysical properties of a location, to analyse 38,591 existing solar sites and the land they were built on to learn the latent solar suitability signal. We assess a set of linear and non-linear models and select a soft-voting ensemble of a random forest and a multilayer perceptron (RF+MLP ensemble), chosen for accuracy and large scale deployability. Validated against future installations in thirteen countries, the ensemble separates existing solar sites from random land with a median ROC-AUC of 0.90. Compared with published MCDA strategies, the ensemble increases ROC-AUC by 0.06-0.30 in every country. The ranking also concentrates real deployment: the most-suitable 20% of land holds 84% of estimated generation (annual energy yield) and 67% of installed capacity (potential power output). After applying standard siting constraints, 5.6% of global land (9.8% if cropland is permitted) remains highly suited to solar. The global 10 m resolution solar suitability dataset and code can be found here: https://github.com/Abdullahr29/Global-Solar-Siting.

items.title: Learning to Restart: Differentiable Restart Policies for Optimization Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2611.08883v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Adaptive restart mechanisms, which reset the momentum or other auxiliary state of an iterative optimizer, play a central role in the empirical performance of accelerated first-order methods, yet existing restart rules remain almost entirely hand-designed. The obstruction to learning restart policies is that, unlike the typical Learning to Optimize (L2O) setting, the discrete restart events make the resulting trajectory non-differentiable in the algorithm parameters and thus block gradient-based optimization of the restart policy. We resolve this obstruction by developing a differentiable framework for restart policies through their continuous-time limit. We introduce surrogate gradients for the restart events and optimization trajectories that are efficient to compute and provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts. We validate the effectiveness of our surrogate gradients in L2O settings, training restart policies that improve upon standard handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs, and that transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.

items.summary: The paper develops a differentiable framework for learning adaptive restart policies in accelerated first-order optimization, overcoming the non-differentiability of discrete restart events via their continuous-time limit and surrogate gradients. This replaces hand-designed restart rules with learned ones.
items.reasoning: Elegant theoretical resolution of a real obstruction in learning-to-optimize, with potential to improve accelerated methods broadly; however, practical gains over well-tuned classical restart rules may be incremental.

items.title: When Can You Trust Neural Critics? Auditing Mutual Information Estimates of Higher-Order Epistasis in Protein Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.09046v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Mutual information (MI) estimation is used to probe what neural representations encode, including in protein language models, but variational MI estimators have variance that scales at least exponentially in the true MI. We audit a prior neural-MI study of order-resolved epistasis in ESM-2 on the four-site GB1 landscape. Run-to-run differences show no systematic bias and a magnitude comparable to ordinary cross-seed retraining variability, and the evaluation-pairing scheme shifts scores substantially. At the original dimensionality, two of three alternative estimator families stabilize the estimate across seeds and one does not. In a synthetic calibration at the representation dimensionalities of two other protein language models (a Gaussian channel with known MI; no model representations), all three families recover materially less signal than required, despite correct signal ordering and stable seeds. A control critic given the true signal direction, which also reduces its input to one dimension, recovers 93.3% and 98.7% of the analytic MI at gain 1.5 (at 5,120 and 4,096 dimensions), so the signal is recoverable with privileged information, but the control does not identify why blind estimation fails. We package the checks into a reusable diagnostic protocol and conclude that even a stabilized estimator is not currently sufficient for order-resolved dependence claims made under blind search at this dimensionality and sample size.

items.summary: This audit examines a prior neural mutual-information study of epistasis in ESM-2 on the GB1 protein landscape, finding run-to-run differences comparable to ordinary seed variability and substantial sensitivity to evaluation pairing schemes. It evaluates alternative estimator families for stability and uses synthetic calibrations across representation dimensionalities. The work provides important methodological scrutiny of variational MI estimation in probing neural representations.
items.reasoning: Rigorous auditing and replication-style analysis addressing known exponential variance issues in variational MI estimators; valuable for interpretability and protein-model probing communities, though incremental in nature.

items.title: Safety-Focused Reinforcement Learning Using Risk-Sensitive Coupled Control
items.content: arXiv:2611.09290v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper investigates the coupled control problem within safety-focused reinforcement learning, addressing the essential challenge of achieving optimal performance while ensuring safety in systems operating within complex environments. We define safety as the requirement to prevent the system from reaching undesirable or hazardous states. We propose a coupled control approach that prioritizes safety by employing effective methods to prevent the system from entering unsafe states while optimizing the performance metric, defined as the average cost. We propose a novel problem transformation that reformulates it into a risk-sensitive problem combined with an average reward criterion. We present a two-timescale Q-learning algorithm where in the faster timescale, the algorithm solves a risk-sensitive control problem to ensure safety, while on a slower timescale, the algorithm focuses on average cost control. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of our algorithms, establishing their significance in ensuring safe, optimal control in dynamic environments. We validated the performance of our approach using GridWorld and CarGoal task in Safety Gymnasium.
items.author: Jiabin Lin, Shana Moothedath, Vivek S. Borkar
items.summary: Proposes a coupled control approach to safe reinforcement learning that transforms constrained optimization into a risk-sensitive problem with an average reward criterion, preventing entry into unsafe states while optimizing average cost. A two-timescale Q-learning algorithm is derived to solve the reformulated problem.
items.reasoning: A solid theoretical contribution to safe RL with a novel problem transformation, but the abstract suggests classical control/learning settings rather than scalable deep RL, limiting immediate practical reach.

items.title: k-Volume: a Unified Active Learning Strategy
items.content: arXiv:2611.09388v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In the classification context where revealing the label of a sample is costly, we propose a new Active Learning (AL) strategy named k-Volume (kVol). It randomly selects a sample to be labeled according to the volume of the smallest ball containing its k nearest neighbors. kVol is highly versatile: it can be applied either in the input space or in the output space, and it enjoys the desirable properties of the three main families of AL strategies: density, diversity, and (when performed in the output space) uncertainty. From a theoretical perspective, we establish that kVol is asymptotically equivalent to uniform sampling over the support of the (input or output) data distribution. Based on experiments on various synthetic and real-life tabular datasets and images, we observe that kVol is surprisingly stable: whatever the classifier or the experimental setup, it still lies among the best AL strategies unlike other competitors that fail dramatically. In particular, kVol outperforms state-of-the-art competitors such as CoreSet, TypiClust or Uncertainty on several real-life datasets, at a low computational cost.

items.title: Coordinatewise Epsilon for Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
items.content: arXiv:2611.09596v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Adam estimates second moments coordinatewise, but typically adds the same scalar $\varepsilon$ to every denominator. We study how this shared $\varepsilon$ affects convergence when noise and curvature vary across coordinates. Under coordinatewise finite-$p$ noise moments, $p\in(1,2]$, choosing $\varepsilon_i$ from the noise and curvature bounds for each coordinate attains the heavy-tailed $\ell_1$-stationarity benchmark $O(T^{-\frac{p-1}{3p-2}})$, matching the known optimal time exponent for smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. For $1<2$, Adam with a shared $\varepsilon_t$ admits a lower bound of order $\Omega(T^{-\frac{p-1}{2p}})$. This lower bound holds for every predictable scalar choice of $\eta_t$, $\beta_{1,t}$, $\beta_{2,t}$, and $\varepsilon_t$, precluding a dimension-uniform benchmark rate for this class.

items.summary: Analyzes how Adam's shared scalar epsilon affects convergence when noise and curvature vary across coordinates, showing that coordinatewise epsilon choices attain the optimal heavy-tailed l1-stationarity rate O(T^-(p-1)/(3p-2)), while any predictable shared epsilon admits a lower bound of order Omega(T^-(p-1)/(2p)). Provides theory directly relevant to the ubiquitous Adam optimizer.

items.title: Online Causal Configuration for Networked Systems via Doubly Robust Steady-State Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.09665v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Measurement exploration reveals how interacting local controllers behave but can alter the steady-state regime a network operator seeks to optimize. Exploratory rewards may therefore fail to identify a configuration's no-exploration value: under full exploration, identical logged distributions can conceal different target values. Identification requires accounting for both action-law mismatch and shifts in the steady-state context distribution. We introduce CAUSAL-UCB, which selects configurations using optimistic bounds on target causal values. Its interference-aware clipped doubly robust evaluator produces predecision certificates separating statistical variation from calibrated identification, transport, and temporal-dependence errors. For any finite horizon and predetermined schedule of measurement-exploration rates $\{\eta_t\}$, we prove lower bounds of $\Omega((1+\sum_t\eta_t)^{-1/2})$ on minimax inference error and $\Omega(\sum_t\eta_t)$ on measurement-induced deployment loss in a stationary, potentially slow-mixing family. We bound regret under valid certificates and selected-information growth, and establish an anytime finite-sample certificate with a shared radius for estimation, selection, and reporting in a restricted known-local-interference model. In a high-mismatch benchmark with 24 paired seeds and 200 rounds, CAUSAL-UCB attains target regret of $1.732$ versus $6.326$ for certified IPS-UCB, with deployment gaps of $30.607$ and $23.217$, respectively. Independent-audit coverage tests and trace-driven semi-synthetic studies further assess certificate coverage and deployment trade-offs.

items.title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds
items.content: arXiv:2611.09723v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.

items.title: GenStrain: Multi-Conditional Generative Diffusion Model To Synthesize High-quality Motion and Strain Maps From Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Images
items.content: arXiv:2611.08544v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper presents GenStrain, a novel method for synthesizing high-quality cardiac motion-based strain maps from routinely collected cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. Existing approaches typically rely on image registration to estimate motion (a sequence of displacements) from cine CMR images, but cine CMR presents very sparse trackable intramyocardial features, presenting challenges to estimate intramyocardial motion. An advanced imaging technique, Displacement Encoding with Stimulated Echoes (DENSE) CMR, is considered as the gold standard for strain assessment, but it requires additional acquisitions, which are not ideal for efficient clinical workflows. To address this gap, we introduce GenStrain, a novel framework designed to learn the data distribution of highly accurate cardiac motion captured by DENSE. In particular, we develop a diffusion process in motion space, where spatiotemporal continuity is carefully considered. items.title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
items.content: arXiv:2611.08693v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

items.title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.08987v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.

items.reasoning: Addresses a real deployment bottleneck for vision-language-action models (compute on-robot versus network latency and server capacity) with a sensible systems idea.
