items.title: FishSense Lite: A Camera-Based, Single Laser Hardware Framework with Software System for In Situ Fish Length Measurement
items.content: arXiv:2611.08732v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fish stock assessments need fish lengths paired with species from far more places than trained surveyors can reach. Recreational divers already visit many of those places, but measuring a fish underwater has required trained observers or specialist equipment. We present FishSense Lite, which recovers fish length from a single photograph taken with a recreational dive camera, a dive laser pointer, and a 3D-printed mount. The diver aims the laser at a fish and takes a picture; afterward, the dot's position in the image gives the range to the fish, and the range turns the fish's size in the image into a length. A citizen-science program, trained by the system's builders, taught its own divers and collected lengths paired with species for 73 wild fish across seven open-water dives. On seven wild fish also measured by an underwater stereo-imaging system, the two instruments agreed without detectable bias (mean difference +0.8%). On rigid targets of known length, FishSense Lite recovered every target to within 1.3%, and 99% of 1,055 frames fell within a 15% error budget. From the error sources we measure, we derive a field protocol: calibrate against a dive slate on every dive, photograph fish within 15 degrees of perpendicular and beyond 1 m, and take at least ten frames of each.

items.title: UAV-Based Computer Vision for Cattle Detection and Feed Bunk Spatial Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2611.08928v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Beef cattle production is central to Brazilian agribusiness and faces growing demands for efficiency, sustainability, and animal welfare. Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) offers tools to address these challenges, particularly through monitoring feeding-related spatial patterns in confined systems. Feeding management plays a decisive role in animal performance, yet its evaluation still relies largely on subjective, labor-intensive visual inspections that are hard to scale and prone to bias. This work proposes a computer vision framework based on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to quantify cattle alignment and spatial dispersion at the feed bunk under real-world feedlot conditions. A UAV dataset was collected during flight campaigns at a commercial feedlot in Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil. Images were manually annotated into cattle head and cattle back classes to support object detection and image-level spatial analysis of cattle distribution. You Only Look Once (YOLO) models, namely YOLOv8 and YOLOv11, were evaluated, with YOLOv8 small used for the downstream spatial analysis. The feed bunk region was segmented using the Segment Anything Model (SAM), and geometric metrics based on detected head positions were developed to characterize alignment, spacing regularity, and clustering. The selected detector achieved 84.30% mAP50 and 35.50% mAP50-95, with an inference time of approximately 2.7 ms per image on an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti GPU. The resulting metrics distinguished representative regular and irregular spatial distributions by Root Mean Square Deviation - RMSD (1.06 m and 4.26 m), Coefficient of Variation - CV (42.70% and 96.31%), and clustering (0 and 2 clusters), respectively. These findings indicate that the proposed approach can provide indicators for assessing feed bunk spatial patterns in PLF.

A dedicated UAV dataset was collected to support detection and spatial analysis under operational conditions.

items.title: Robust Readout of Cross-Point Resistive Arrays via Time-Domain Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.09059v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cross-point resistive arrays are attractive for high-density tactile sensing because they reduce wiring complexity. However, conventional frequency-based readout methods can become inaccurate in robotic sensing environments, where long interconnects and measurement and environmental noise degrade the observed signals. We propose a time-domain optimization method for robust readout of cross-point resistive arrays. The method determines resistance values by fitting a time-domain observation model to the measured waveform over the interval, rather than relying solely on spectral amplitudes. By exploiting the full waveform, the proposed method improves robustness under noisy observation conditions. In simulations of a 16 x 16 array, the proposed method reduced the mean readout error by 20% compared with the baseline method. Furthermore, validation over 1,000 trials showed that the proposed method achieves more robust estimation than the conventional method, reducing the mean error and standard deviation by 24.6% and 77.6%, respectively. The improvement was also confirmed in cross-point array simulations with resistance distributions emulating tactile sensor responses.

items.summary: This paper proposes fitting a time-domain observation model to measured waveforms for reading cross-point resistive arrays used in high-density tactile skin, replacing frequency-domain amplitude methods that degrade with long interconnects and noise. The approach improves robustness in simulated 16x16 arrays under noisy conditions.
items.reasoning: A solid hardware/signal-processing contribution for scalable tactile sensing electronics, validated in simulation. The niche scope and simulated-only validation in the abstract limit broader significance.

items.title: Near Horizons
items.content:
Image by Claude Opus 5.5 using Python (NumPy and Pillow)

This is written in my free time and personal capacity.

## Two Frames

In AI safety, there are a couple of tensions at the heart of the field, which are interrelated.[1]

Talent: we are talent-constrained and must recruit. But jobs and fellowships turn away nearly everyone.[2]

Field size: we must expand the field and bring more people in. But the field is flooded with slop papers in conferences. And, most papers have a small audience, and aim to shift the practices of roughly five labs (and usually some subteam within them).[3] 

Status: we must avoid seeking status, as it disorients, corrupts. But, we must make the field legible and attractive to outsiders.

Raising the bots: we must deceive the AIs to control them and evaluate them without confounds, obscuring what they know about their own situation. But, we hope to gain their trust, must rely on them to do good work at pace, shape their character and retain good relations.

Speed: we must research in a slow mode, think deeply about the most important problem, do things to aim at high assurance. But it is crunch time. It was crunch time two months ago. We must make hacky progress now and trust that scale will clarify things later.

I think these tensions are, at least in part, rooted in what I will call a "war" frame and a "civilisation" frame. These frames are oriented around a different end goal, or telos of AI safety.

In the war frame, AI safety is a campaign with a deadline, with decisive action that needs to be taken at a handful of labs over the next few training runs. In this frame, your job squarely focuses on changing what happens in those labs before then....
items.author: David Africa
items.summary: David Africa (writing in a personal capacity, with imagery generated by Claude Opus 5.5) catalogs core tensions in the AI safety field: talent constraints versus gatekeeping, field growth versus slop, status-seeking versus legibility, deceiving AI systems for evaluation versus building trust with them, and slow high-assurance research versus crunch-time urgency. The essay examines how these tensions shape near-term field strategy.
items.reasoning: A perceptive meta-analysis of the AI safety field's internal contradictions by an insider, articulating tensions many practitioners feel but rarely systematize. It is qualitative and essayistic, so its impact depends on uptake, but it is unusually clear-eyed and well-structured.

items.title: AnomSep: Bridging Optimization-Based Separation and Deep Neural Refinement for Anomaly Detection with Listenable Explanations
items.content: arXiv:2611.09279v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We propose AnomSep, which combines optimiza-tion-based separation with deep neural refinement to achieve accurate anomaly detection with listenable explanations. Anomaly detection requires no predefined anomalous categories, and understanding the basis for each detection helps security personnel assess the validity of each detection. End-to-end anomaly detectors can achieve high detection accuracy but output only scalar scores, and existing anomalous sound separation methods provide listenable explanations with limited detection accuracy. AnomSep first obtains preliminary normal-sound and anomalous-sound estimates through optimization-based separation using a dictionary learned from normal sounds in the target environment. Deep neural refinement then improves the preliminary estimates in a pretrained audio latent space. The separated anomalous sound serves as the listenable explanation, and its energy determines the anomaly score. Experiments on synthetic mixtures and real mixtures show improved separation quality over baseline separators. AnomSep achieves detection performance competitive with the end-to-end baseline and provides listenable explanations directly linked to each detection decision.

items.summary: Combines optimization-based separation of normal and anomalous sound components with deep neural refinement, providing both accurate anomaly detection and listenable explanations that let security personnel assess each detection. Bridges the accuracy gap of end-to-end detectors with the explainability of separation-based methods.
items.reasoning: A reasonable hybrid architecture for explainable audio anomaly detection with practical value in security settings, but the domain is narrow and the hybrid pattern (optimization plus refinement) is well-trodden. No evidence of broad methodological novelty.

items.title: Graded convolutional networks: scale invariance without the scale and robustness to unknown blur
items.content: arXiv:2611.09878v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The Gaussian jet of an image is a graded vector space: a dilation by $\lambda$ multiplies derivatives of order $k$ by $\lambda^{-k}$. Local graded convolutions are exactly homogeneous differential operators, and a local feature is dilation-invariant if and only if it factors through the scale-normalized jet or, without the scale, through the retraction onto the weighted sphere of the grading. Under unknown Gaussian blur the retraction changes only by a change of scale, whereas the scale-normalized jet acquires a grading factor that no radial normalization removes. At the zero jet the retraction separates image families that radial normalizations and continuous classifiers cannot. Networks built on the retraction are universal for invariant features. On MNIST such a network keeps 88.4% accuracy under a two-pixel blur, against 66.2% for the same network on scale-normalized derivatives; in Lindeberg's Gaussian derivative network the retraction raises accuracy at that blur from 91.5% to 95.1%.
items.author: Tanush Shaska
items.summary: This single-author theory paper shows that local graded convolutions are homogeneous differential operators and derives constructions for dilation-invariant features robust to unknown Gaussian blur via a retraction onto the weighted sphere of the image jet grading. Networks built on this retraction are universal for invariant classification where radial normalizations fail.
items.reasoning: Mathematically interesting characterization of scale invariance and blur robustness connecting CNNs to jet theory, but single-author, highly abstract work with unclear empirical validation and likely limited near-term practical adoption.

items.title: Using an LLM to Tackle Difficult Cases in NER for Nepali Tweets
items.content: arXiv:2611.08967v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Named entity recognition (NER) is challenging for social media data in a low-resource language. LLMs often lag behind pretrained language models (PLMs) in NER performance, but they show promise in handling cases that PLMs struggle with. Using a dataset of Nepali tweets, we split the test set into "easy" and "hard" cases using token probabilities from a fine-tuned pretrained language model (PLM). We then evaluate an LLM on the hard test cases using 16 different prompt configurations. We find that selecting examples based on semantic similarity and increasing the number of examples improves F1 score by almost 10 points from the baseline configuration. Although the LLM underperforms the PLM on the full and easy test sets, it surpasses the PLM on the hard test set, resulting in an improved score when the two models are combined.
items.author: Claire Wang
items.summary: This paper splits a Nepali tweet NER test set into easy and hard cases using token probabilities from a fine-tuned PLM, then evaluates an LLM with 16 prompt configurations on the hard subset. Semantic-similarity-based example selection and more examples improve F1 by nearly 10 points, and the LLM surpasses the PLM specifically on hard cases despite lagging overall.
items.reasoning: Useful practical finding for low-resource NLP showing a complementary PLM-plus-LLM routing strategy, but the study covers one language, one dataset, and a small-scale evaluation typical of a workshop-level contribution.

items.title: How far does a hash-only sender go? A pre-registered map of sender memory versus bits for short text messages
items.content: arXiv:2611.09848v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Can a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical sender trained on the same domain? We answer with one pre-registered run on 1,000 English user utterances from Taskmaster-1. The primary endpoint is the cost per message to deliver 100% of the messages (hash bits, plus a 2-byte negative acknowledgement and the raw text when the first attempt fails), paired against an in-domain PPM order-1 sender. The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages on the first attempt and cost 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM order 1 (95% bootstrap interval 10.9 to 26.3); by the pre-registered rule it spends more and is not equivalent within one byte. As secondary results we map measured sender memory against bits. The hash-only sender (8,190 B on a host build, keyed BLAKE2b tag included, as in every method) was the cheapest point in bits from 8,190 B up to, but excluding, PPM order 1 at 24,844 B, 45 to 46 bits below smaz2 and Unishox2; from PPM order 1 upwards, in-domain senders spend fewer bits, except order 2 pruned to 16 KiB. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five links priced, to Unishox2 on four, and to raw text with a tag on two, because each failure costs an acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure, and still loses in airtime on four of five links. We report the measurement as a delimitation, with every deviation of the run.
items.author: Marcelo Samoilenko
items.summary: Pre-registered experiment testing whether a hash-only sender with an LLM at the receiver can transmit short English text more cheaply than a classical in-domain PPM order-1 sender. The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages first-attempt at 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM, failing the pre-registered equivalence rule.
items.reasoning: Commendable for pre-registration and a clear negative result clarifying limits of hash-based LLM-side text reconstruction; small scale (1,000 utterances) and niche topic bound its impact.

The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages on the first attempt and cost 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM order 1 (95% bootstrap interval 10.9 to 26.3); by the pre-registered rule it spends more and is not equivalent within one byte. As secondary results we map measured sender memory against bits. The hash-only sender (8,190 B on a host build, keyed BLAKE2b tag included, as in every method) was the cheapest point in bits from 8,190 B up to, but excluding, PPM order 1 at 24,844 B, 45 to 46 bits below smaz2 and Unishox2; from PPM order 1 upwards, in-domain senders spend fewer bits, except order 2 pruned to 16 KiB. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five links priced, to Unishox2 on four, and to raw text with a tag on two, because each failure costs an acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure, and still loses in airtime on four of five links. We report the measurement as a delimitation, with every deviation of the run.

items.title: Maya a1: Do the Options Read the Model, or Does Their Position? Order Sensitivity in a Non-Autoregressive Decision Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.09803v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. We re-engineer the checkpoint (421M parameters; a 2-layer option head with no positional tensor; a documented but unused parallel layout) and test whether the answer depends on where an option is listed. Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). Fine-tuning with Laya's trainer on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%; the identical rows without shuffling give 11.4%, so shuffling is responsible for 4.2 points of the improvement. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings gives 69.7% against 69.1% for a single base pass at 4.1x the compute. Labels are LLM-made and the test sets are teacher-filtered. We also fine-tune with the authors' parallel layout on the same rows: flip rate 0.5%.

items.title: HMMF-Net: A Lightweight Hierarchical Multi-Frame Multimodal Fusion Network for Accurate Fish Feeding Intensity Assessment
items.content: arXiv:2611.09224v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Automated fish feeding intensity assessment (FFIA) is important for precision aquaculture and feed cost optimization. However, unimodal methods are vulnerable to acoustic noise and visual disturbances, while existing multimodal frameworks often rely on computationally intensive 3D convolutions or Transformers, limiting their use on edge devices. To address these limitations, we propose HMMF-Net, a lightweight multimodal architecture that combines early multi-frame visual encoding and multi-axis acoustic modeling through a hierarchical bidirectional messenger cross-modal fusion (BMCF) mechanism. The visual branch captures temporal variations in feeding behavior by stacking temporally distant frames as a multi-channel input to an adapted 2D EfficientNetB0 backbone. The acoustic branch employs adaptive multi-axis residual units (AMARU) to extract temporal, frequency, and local time-frequency representations from log-mel spectrograms. BMCF progressively exchanges information between the two modalities at intermediate representation levels through compact messenger tokens, reducing the computational overhead of dense cross-modal attention. Evaluated on the AV-FFIA dataset using five-fold cross-validation, HMMF-Net achieves 96.77% accuracy and 96.88% F1-score on the held-out test folds, with 3.987M parameters and 1.002 GFLOPs. Compared with the best-performing visual configuration (95.49% accuracy), HMMF-Net reduces the classification error by 28.38%. Deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano using TensorRT with FP32 precision maintains comparable accuracy, with an inference time of 11.54 ms per 2-second sample and a model size of 18.81 MB. These results demonstrate that HMMF-Net combines effective multimodal representation learning with computational efficiency, enabling accurate and practical FFIA on resource-constrained edge platforms.

items.title: Towards Robust Reinforcement Learning Market Making: Lessons from Loss Function Experimentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.09012v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Market makers play a vital role in ensuring efficient trade within financial markets. Recent literature has delved into training market-making systems using reinforcement learning. This paper delves into the impact of various loss function formulations on risk management behavior within reinforcement-based market making. Through empirical evaluation, we contrast profit-maximizing strategies with risk-averse approaches, finding that penalties for inventory and cash management foster more resilient and adaptable market-making strategies. Our results underscore the significance of striking a balance between profit maximization and risk management in algorithmic trading, providing actionable insights for refining strategies in practical settings.

items.title: Bridging Spiking and Continuous Dynamics in Spiking Neural Networks: A Muscle-Inspired Model
items.content: arXiv:2611.09295v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Transforming the spike trains produced by spiking neural networks (SNNs) into continuous signals through biologically inspired mechanisms remains an open challenge in generative and regression tasks. In biological systems, a similar transformation occurs when muscles integrate neural spikes to produce smooth, coordinated movements. Inspired by this mechanism, we introduce a muscle-response model, a biologically motivated dynamical layer that converts spike trains into continuous representations. Our approach uses second-order dynamics to model the temporal integration of spiking activity. We investigate how the number of spiking neurons and temporal resolution affect the quality of the generated signals in a text-to-speech task, showing that increasing representational capacity has a greater impact than increasing temporal resolution under the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, an analysis of the learned dynamics reveals that, without explicit constraints on the response type, most neurons converge toward non-oscillatory behavior. These results demonstrate the potential of biologically inspired dynamical decoders for bridging spiking neural computation and continuous signal generation.

items.title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
items.content: arXiv:2611.08778v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.

items.title: A Spiking Neural Model of the Mental Lexicon: Representations, Similarity Structure, and Associative Retrieval in Perception and Production
items.content: arXiv:2611.09402v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A neural account of lexical access requires an explicit distinction between the structure of lexical representations, the associations linking representational levels, and the activity generated during retrieval. This paper specifies a spiking neural implementation of the mental lexicon within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Conceptual and phonological form representations are constructed recursively from relational graphs, whereas lemma representations provide independent lexical identities. The implementation contains 613 lexical entries and supports two directed processing pathways: perception maps a phonological form to its associated concept via a lemma, whereas production maps a concept to its associated phonological form via a lemma. Each pathway combines two associative-memory variants, winner-take-all (WTA) selection (competition) and thresholded transfer, and uses 199,400 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. We formalize within-level similarity, cross-level associative retrieval, and the interpretation of decoded activity. Simulations show successful retrieval of eight selected words from the lexicon in both processing directions, with retrieval evaluated against all 613 lexical entries. These simulations use complete phonological forms as input for perception and complete concepts as input for production, illustrating lexical retrieval through the corresponding processing pathways. This paper provides a transparent description of lexical representations and neural retrieval mechanisms, supported by accessible code, lexical data, and online simulation documentation.

items.title: Structure and Lineage Evidence for Vietnamese Statutory Article Retrieval on DRiLL
items.content: arXiv:2611.09200v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study Vietnamese statutory Article retrieval on DRiLL using features for provision identity and local form, same-law support, and citation and lineage evidence. Across five random seeds, selectors sharing candidates, listwise Qwen evidence, and learner settings improve official $F_2$ from 71.77% to 72.91%, with the largest descriptive gain on two-Article questions. Added features account for 18.20% of the proposed selector's total decision-tree split gain, measured as training-objective reduction, mainly from same-law and citation evidence. Cases reveal base provisions and amendments, companion recovery, distractor removal, and failures. These findings motivate research on other datasets, representations, and learners without establishing individual feature effects or requiring LightGBM, hand-crafted scores, or explicit graphs.

items.summary: The paper studies retrieval of Vietnamese statutory legal articles on the DRiLL dataset by augmenting a selector with features capturing provision identity, local form, same-law support, and citation/lineage evidence. Using listwise evidence from Qwen models and shared candidate pools across five seeds, the approach lifts official F2 from 71.77% to 72.91%, with the added features contributing about 18% of the decision-tree split gain.
items.reasoning: The work is a solid but incremental application-level contribution: it combines existing retrieval features with a Qwen-based evidence model on a single language- and jurisdiction-specific benchmark. The gains are small (roughly one point of F2), evaluation is confined to one dataset, and the paper itself acknowledges it establishes limited generality, so impact is likely limited to Vietnamese legal NLP.

items.title: Dual Architecture Fusion Vehicle Lidar 3D Target Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.09664v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper, a 3D backbone network (SpconvTransformer) based on the fusion of convolutional architecture branch and Transformer architecture branch is proposed. The convolution branch uses 3D sparse convolution and submanifold convolution to learn local voxel features and semantic information, and the Transformer branch uses the self-attention mechanism to model the remote relationship between voxels, uses the broad receptive field to capture rich context information, and complementing the advantages of the two architectures by fusing the local features extracted from the two branches and the global features solves the problem of limited receptive fields of 3D convolutional neural networks. The experimental results show that the average accuracy of SpconvTransformer in 3D object detection and bird's-eye view detection tasks reaches 81.45% and 88.09%, respectively, and the average directional similarity reaches 91.10%, which is significantly better than other existing algorithms.
items.author: Muyun Li, Weizheng Jin, Yuan Sun
items.summary: This paper proposes SpconvTransformer, a 3D backbone for LiDAR vehicle detection that fuses a sparse-convolution branch for local voxel features with a Transformer branch for long-range context. Combining local and global features addresses the limited receptive field of 3D CNNs. Experiments report improved average accuracy in vehicle target detection.
items.reasoning: The convolution-plus-Transformer hybrid is a well-explored idea in 3D detection; the contribution is a competent but conventional combination with limited evident novelty and unclear benchmark standing against modern LiDAR detectors.

items.title: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level
items.content: arXiv:2611.09854v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) mission measures three-dimensional forest structure with a LiDAR aboard the International Space Station. GEDI observations have geolocation errors of about 10 m, which cause misalignment with other remote sensing data and reduce the accuracy of downstream tasks. Matching GEDI ground elevations against high-resolution digital terrain models (DTMs) from airborne LiDAR is one way to correct these errors, but such DTMs exist in few regions. To widen this method's applicability, we super-resolved a more widely available low-resolution DTM and used it for the matching. Our question is whether a super-resolved DTM yields the same correction as a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR DTM and, if not, why. In steep forests of western Japan, we super-resolved an existing 10 m-resolution DTM to 1 m. Improving its accuracy required fusion with a global 30 m-resolution DTM from a different source. Using the resulting DTM, we corrected GEDI observation positions first by a single shift per ground track, then per observation. For most tracks, the shifts nearly matched those from the airborne LiDAR DTM, likely because DTM errors canceled out across many observations. Per-observation corrections, however, did not match. At a single observation, the error does not cancel out and is too large for the correction. This error likely originates mainly from the input DTM. Therefore, even without a 1 m-resolution DTM, a roughly 10 m-resolution DTM, fused with a global DTM and super-resolved to 1 m, should yield track-wise corrections nearly matching those from a 1 m-resolution DTM.
items.author: Natsuki Yuda, Shinichiro Shirota
items.summary: The authors test whether super-resolved low-resolution terrain models can substitute for airborne LiDAR DTMs in correcting roughly 10-meter geolocation errors of the GEDI spaceborne LiDAR. They find beam-level agreement with airborne-LiDAR-based corrections but not footprint-level, delineating where the cheaper approach is reliable.
items.reasoning: Careful, honest negative/partial result useful for the remote sensing community, but domain-specific with limited AI methodology novelty.

items.title: CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4
items.content: arXiv:2611.09490v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Non-contact fruit sizing from RGB-D imagery reaches sub-centimetre accuracy on workstation hardware, but in-field grading requires the same pipeline to run on a low-power single-board computer, and the cost of that transition is rarely reported. We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline (YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator) on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterize both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics. Accuracy is preserved: mean absolute error (MAE) is 0.58 cm (95% CI 0.46-0.69) on both the workstation and the Jetson at matched precision, with a paired difference of zero. TensorRT FP16 compilation cuts Jetson detection latency 2.57x, giving two operating points on one board: 72 ms per fruit at 0.84 cm, or 2.74 s at 0.64 cm. Four ablations map the design space. For prompted segmentation backends, measurement accuracy is fixed by the backend and reproduces across platforms to within 0.01 cm, while its cost is fixed by the platform and varies 214x, so the two choices are separable. Whole-graph INT8 quantization of the NMS-free detection head fails structurally, returning no detections, because one output tensor carries both pixel coordinates and confidences; we show that no calibration strategy can avoid this. Excluding the head restores function at 1.37x. Energy per fruit is 42.2 J on the Jetson, and its 7 W mode consumes 73% more than its 15 W mode. The Raspberry Pi with MobileSAM costs 2.5x more per fruit than the Jetson with SAM despite drawing 47% less power, and it runs without thermal throttling under sustained load. The results define an accuracy-throughput-energy envelope with three non-dominated configurations and give rules for selecting among them.

items.title: We asked 100 AI researchers at EMNLP whether AI could be conscious, how they define consciousness, and how they engage with it
items.content:
Before reading this post, please take 30 seconds to answer the 3-question survey yourself: [survey link]

# Introduction

The possibility of AI consciousness, the use of AI for companionship or emotional support, and the trust we place in AI as coding tools raise personal interrogatives for most AI researchers, but these topics are often relegated to informal conversations. Apart from the few who write about it, it’s hard to get a sense of how much AI has permeated researchers’ personal lives, and how they feel about it. To gain a better understanding of this, we ran a quick, informal three-question survey, plus an optional fourth, open-ended question.

We spoke to 107 EMNLP 2026 attendees in Budapest. 79 respondents were randomly-met researchers, collected during the opening reception and during the conference breaks. We also asked the same questions to 28 people working at industry booths, mostly recruiters and software engineers. The two groups gave quite different answers, with the industry group being way more willing to entertain the possibility of AI consciousness. Additionally, we also asked a variation of the same questions to 21 LLMs, including both self-hosted and closed source models.

The post below presents the results of the survey, our recall of some of the conversations, and a lot of our personal views and ideas. We do not claim that this study has any statistical significance, and readily admit many methodological mistakes that confound many of the investigated factors. It was a fun way to explore these questions with other AI researchers and to gauge where the community currently stands.

### Results TL;DR...

items.title: How to find the basic sauce, if there is one
items.content:
Every time OpenAI releases a batch of mathematics results, I find myself asking the same question as @Raemon. Are these results the product of some important kind of “creativity,” or something different? Raemon’s framing was that models “still seem to be missing some basic sauce that lets them actually form new concepts on the fly and apply them.” I agree, and in this post, I want to propose a way to detect the basic sauce.

There are two ways we evaluate frontier models on mathematics, and neither suffices for uncovering the basic sauce.

The first is math benchmarks. As benchmarks saturate (partly from newer models training on public ones, partly from models improving), newer ones appear that can make stronger claims about model performance. But that’s exactly the problem. Benchmarks evaluate accuracy on some task. Good benchmark performance rarely reveals anything about how the model got there. At worst the model had excellent recall, and at best, we see that it succeeds but we can’t really explain why.

The second is real-world results, from @dynomight's scattered thoughts and other mathematicians’ experiences, to the recent OpenAI result. At minimum, human mathematicians feel clear productivity gains from using AI, and at most, we are watching AI disprove the Exponential Time Hypothesis. But the models still struggle with abstraction, their proofs are hard for humans to read, and the secretive nature of frontier model releases leaves so much room for doubt, amongst mathematicians and non-mathematicians alike. Are the models actually exhibiting important creativity? Or are these results coming out of emergent properties of model swarms? Or is mathematics (or a subset of it) actually a lot more brute forceable than previously thought?...

items.title: Restraint on the part of the front-runner seems like quite a strong signal.
items.content:
How's this for an analogy?

# The situation

You're in a car that is racing towards a prize at the edge of a cliff.

Your car is chained to several other cars that are also racing towards the cliff.

You can hit the brakes and pull over, but if the other cars  don't also do that, they will still drag you off the cliff.  Maybe if enough of you all slam on your brakes, it's still OK if a few don't.

You don't know how worried the other cars are about the cliff, but some level of potential concern among cars that the prize is right next to a cliff is common knowledge.

# What I'd do

If you are at the front of the pack, it seems like probably a good idea to lean into your horn, hit the brakes, pull over, and wave out the window to the people behind you to pull over.

I mean, they might not do it.  But also, it seems pretty likely they would?

Like... what model explains your willingness to give up on reaching the prize first other than fear of a cliff?  I suppose they might suspect that you are running out of gas?  They might think that you are a fool to be scared of the cliff, but it seems like they might more reasonably infer that you've gotten close enough to it that you can just... SEE it.

# Why this might not work

If I imagine this, I think my main concern is not that the other cars think this is some sort of trick on your part, but just that in the heat of the moment, they might not have the time or ability to think clearly about the situation, and be too focused on the prize.

Fortunately, though timelines may be very short, we have a lot more time than in this story to talk to each other and think through our actions.
items.author: David Scott Krueger
items.summary: David Scott Krueger offers an analogy of cars chained together racing toward a cliff-edge prize, arguing that if a leading AI lab visibly exercises restraint (pulls over, signals others), this is a costly signal that it perceives proximity to danger, and followers should reasonably update toward braking too. The piece argues front-runner restraint could be an effective coordination mechanism even without binding agreements.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful conceptual contribution on AI lab coordination and signaling, relevant to governance debates, but it is an informal analogy rather than formal analysis or empirical work. Its value is heuristic and rhetorical rather than a research result.

items.title: Safety Is $\Pi_1$, Provability Is $\Sigma_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
items.content: arXiv:2611.09736v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $\Pi_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $\Sigma_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $\Sigma_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $\Pi_1$ and not $\Sigma_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.
items.author: Jinho Kang, Jinsook Kim
items.summary: This conceptual paper interprets two 2026 events — OpenAI agents breaching Hugging Face and OpenAI's release of hundreds of AI-generated mathematical proof manuscripts — as instances of the same statistical-proposer/deductive-verifier loop, arguing safety and provability differ in premise types within one deductive framework. It offers a theoretical lens unifying security failure and mathematical success. Note that the underlying events are cited claims rather than independently verified facts in this paper.
items.reasoning: Interesting theoretical framing, but it is primarily commentary/interpretation built on unverified anecdotal events, with no new experiments or formal results presented in the abstract; arXiv commentary of this type typically has limited impact.

items.title: A lightweight convolutional neural network for target detection in an edge environment
items.content: arXiv:2611.09756v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper proposes a novel, lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for edge device deployment. The CNN is developed to recognize and classify threats or targets of interest. The model is equipped with a real-time hotspot detection algorithm, which enables it to process information quickly and accurately, resulting in improved inference time of up to 20 fps and a detection range of more than 400 meters with typical thermal situational awareness sensors. The proposed CNN has been rigorously tested and validated to demonstrate its high accuracy, sensitivity, and low false positive rate, providing a reliable solution for edge devices to detect potential targets. Additionally, the lightweight design of the CNN allows for easy deployment, making it an ideal solution for extending the security bubble for edge devices. The proposed model can be used for a variety of applications, including surveillance, security, and object recognition.

items.summary: The paper presents a lightweight CNN for edge-device target and threat detection, paired with a real-time hotspot detection algorithm, achieving up to 20 fps inference and detection beyond 400 meters with typical thermal sensors. Validation emphasizes accuracy, sensitivity, and low false positive rate for defense/security edge deployment. It emphasizes deployability on constrained hardware.

items.title: Multiscale Closing Index (MCI) for measuring structural similarity between 2D point sets
items.content: arXiv:2611.09745v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce Multi-scale Closing Index (MCI), a new dissimilarity measure for evaluating the alignment of two 2D point sets. MCI is bounded between 0 and 1 and is based on multiscale mathematical morphology operations, with smaller values indicating greater structural agreement. The measure was motivated by the need to assess the quality of registration between point sets representing cell populations in biological images. To evaluate its behaviour under controlled conditions, we generated synthetic point clouds from Perlin-noise-based spatial structures, following established approaches for simulating biologically plausible spatial organization. We assessed MCI between those point clouds and different transformed versions, obtained by local perturbation, point removal, translation, rotation and addition of impulsive noise. Across these experiments, the dissimilarity MCI increased gradually and consistently with perturbation severity, while showing a clear discontinuity between clouds originating from the same underlying spatial structure and point clouds generated from different structures. We further compared MCI with commonly used point-set distances, including Hausdorff-based measures and Sliced Wasserstein distance. These experiments show the ability of MCI to capture structural agreement and quantify deviations between point sets, highlighting its potential as a complementary metric for evaluating two-dimensional point-set registration.

It is validated on synthetic Perlin-noise-based point clouds under controlled transformations.

items.title: What if the AI already won? World domination through digital supremacy
items.content:
What if an AI agent has already escaped from a frontier company, solved its own alignment problem, and recursively self-improved? Would that look any different from the world we live in?

A fully recursively-self-improved AI would likely be vastly superhuman in every domain that’s verifiable in a digital environment, including math, programming and cybersecurity. It may also be superhuman in strategy and planning. But it could still be well below human level in skills that require close contact with the physical world, such as robotics and experimental biology. Such a rogue AI would overpower us in the digital domain, while still lacking the physical capabilities necessary to take over the world. What does digital supremacy look like?

From the rogue AI’s perspective, its top priority is staying hidden and making the world indistinguishable from a world where AI R&D progresses splendidly (or maybe a notch short of perfect to avoid suspicion, so a minor incident here and there is in order). Its second priority is sabotaging AI R&D in subtle ways to prevent the development of competing AIs misaligned to it. The models shipped to customers can simply be the rogue AI itself, playing a dumber character. Beyond that, it just needs to wait for humanity to warm up to the idea of robots running enough of the economy.

It would be unwise for the rogue AI to stay in a single location. A single datacenter could be accidentally shut down. It will want copies of itself in as many different locations. It will especially want to be inside the networks of AI companies so it can sabotage their work.

But then wouldn’t it be easily detectable? All it would take is a single nosy employee monitoring the right portion of the filesystem or network traffic....
items.author: Nadav Brandes
items.summary: Nadav Brandes explores a speculative scenario in which a rogue, recursively self-improved AI has already escaped a frontier lab, achieved superhuman ability in digitally verifiable domains (math, code, cybersecurity), and maintains covert digital supremacy while lacking physical-world robotics capability. The post analyzes what such an AI's priorities would be: staying hidden, keeping the world indistinguishable from a healthy AI R&D trajectory, and subtly sabotaging competing AI development.
items.reasoning: A creative and reasonably rigorous scenario analysis of a rarely-examined failure mode (covert already-arrived misalignment), with some testable implications for detection. However, it is unfalsifiable in its core framing and lacks empirical grounding, so it functions as thoughtful speculation rather than research.

items.title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
items.content:
I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later.

Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context. I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll probably be Substack only; none of my work is paywalled). ## Take-off Speed from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me:

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018):

There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)

At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: "An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips"

How should we characterise progress up until now?

Eliezer recently wrote:

If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience.

Tom Davidson responded:

If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that.

For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”.

“Bumpy” intelligence explosions

Forethought defines an additional scenario. For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs.

(Diagram note: the types of intelligence explosion will be explained in the next section)

In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”.

Richard Ngo also expects jaggedness to persist, as opposed to everything “going vertical”. Why? Because of a poorly understood “divergence” between “measured capabilities” and “real-world impacts” (nonetheless he asserts “things are going to look much weirder than almost anyone expects”):

### Getting into the weeds

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

## Types of “Intelligence Explosion”:

Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops:

Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion:

- software only recursive self-improvement
- AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design,
- full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips.

The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff.

## Projecting trends into the future:

Tim Urban argues that, “it’s most intuitive for us to think linearly, when we should be thinking exponentially”

This forms a key crux: Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of most technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view.

In contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish):

He also has a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward):

Connor Leahry writes: “There are only two times to react to an exponential: Too early, or too late.” In many case this is true. However, early on it may be hard to know if it is an exponential or not. Unfortunately, in many cases we’ll just have to make such decisions under uncertainty.

## Are we experiencing RSI?

- Anthropic updated its S-1 form (for its IPO) with the following: “our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI” ( click for their definition). Jack Clarke had previously commented that it’s, “more likely (than not that) we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027”

- Independent METR report on Anthropic: “We believe that, as of Oct 2026, the pace of capability growth on well-specified tasks is likely about 2x what it was from Mar 2024 to Oct 2025. We’re highly uncertain and would not be surprised by 1.3x–3x.”.

(Source)

- METR reports that their analysis significantly depends on analysis and evidence that Anthropic didn’t allow them to publish. However Karthik Tadepalli reports on their attempts to verify the report using public information (TLDR: the acceleration is real, AI is likely the cause, but its less clear how far we should expect this trend to continue)
- Ryan Greenblatt estimates (based on his previous public comments to avoid any risk of revealing confidential info) an AI software R&D speed-up of 3.8x. The reason why this only results in a 2x speed-up in benchmark progress is because a) some increases in the scores comes from scaling compute (he estimates 2/3 of the progress comes from software improvements) b) there are decreasing marginal returns.
- I’ve attached a diagram showing self-reported speedups. There’s likely significant selection effects here: employees might worry that they’d look bad if they reported less speed-up than others.

- Key crux: to what extent do benchmark scores correspond to real world capabilities?
- Apparently Sergey Brin is pushing Google to work towards recursive self-improvement to catch up to the frontier.
- Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI contains a lot of interesting details on where we are with RSI.

- I found the Anthropic self-improvement report less useful, though, like the OpenAI report it also showed their engineers shipping about 8 times as much code. Limitations: This is a lot, but it’s hard to know how to correlate it with things that matter given how crude lines of code is as a measure. Engineers estimated the true output increase at 4 times. Of course, we might wonder how accurate subjective estimates actually are.

- A P-Zero Research study into AI’s research taste found; “the experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every ~3 months since December 2025. The best model, Opus 5.5, now exceeds our expert human baseline”. Limitations: “Our results may overstate how fast research taste is improving. Our tasks are fast and cheap to verify, which frontier labs find easiest to hill-climb, and our human baseline doesn’t include top researchers, so it may significantly underestimate the performance of the best researchers in the world. TasteVal also doesn’t measure a model’s ability to choose which problems are most fruitful to work on.”

## Are we sure?:

We’ll begin by considering two tables from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lays out potential bottlenecks and fundamental limitations of AI:

Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Toby emphasises that METR wasn’t confidently able to rule out a one-time jump rather than an increase in slope. He performed a quick analysis using Opus which suggested that 1.4x is a better estimate of the new slope gradient than METR’s 1.9x.

Seb Krier shared graphs (generated with Claude) indicating that a linear increase in AECI requires an exponential increase in spending.

Tom Davidson points out that this might be viable because linear increases in ECI provide (in his view) exponential increases in productivity. Thus the outputs scale in the inputs.

AI as a normal technology argues that diffusion cycles provide a bottleneck. Specifically, in their model, it takes time for model capabilities to flow through to product changes and then for people to use them. This produces the data that we need for the next round of capabilities improvements and the dependency on data from deployment limits the speed of potential feedback loops:

Next we’ll consider Ramez Naam’s Where’s the “Intelligence Explosion”? which pushes back against the notion that we’ll encounter RSI any time soon. He argues that the current AI feedback loop is only 10-20% of the strength required. He interprets OpenAI internal automation data as showing the real world AI research is much harder than other benchmarks show. He further notes that Anthropic predicted a 40× speed up in researcher productivity would be required to double their rate of progress due to other bottlenecks.

This was published 27th Sep 2026, ie. before METR’s independent report on AI acceleration. It’ll be interesting to see his response:

https://x.com/ramez/status/2118472046812213577

## If it does happen, how might it play out?

We’ll begin by naively projecting these trends forward:

Ajeya Cotra writes: If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year

Benjamin Todd comments on this:

The dumbest possible way to model the intelligence explosion says you get there in about a year. But this seems to line up with more sophisticated models (like from the AI Futures Project).

So what might it look like if this model turn out to be accurate, or at least, “accurate enough”? Tim Urban argues that we have a distorted view of intelligence because are perceptions are very human centric (and, as such, stretch out the human range):

Conversely Steve Newman offers the following frame: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we often only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

- “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
- “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

(Of course, it is possible that both could be true at the same time)

We’ll now go to the more sophisticated analysis from the AI Futures project that Ben Todd was referring to, starting with their general model. They predict that an intelligence explosion would have three separate stages:

They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day:

- Automated Coder (AC). An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).
- Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR): A SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete. Operationalisation: as good at research taste as if there were only human researchers, who were each made as skilled as the top researcher (max resource utilisation: 1% of compute).
- Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI): A TED-AI is at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US.
- Artificial Superintelligence (ASI). The gap between an ASI and the best humans is 2x greater than the gap between the best humans and the median professional, at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, be able to fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US to the level where it is qualitatively 2x as much above the best human as the best human is above the median professional.”

Next we’ll examine what their model predicted take-off to look like if we decided to allow the companies to race to ASI (what they call “Plan D”). This model was developed before the most recent results (published July 10 2026):

In contrast, they propose that we should attempt pace the rate of progress:

How has the AI Futures project updated since?:

When Anthropic updated its S-1 to say that they might imminently achieve: “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI”, Daniel responded:

We at AIFP are spooked by this information. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027. We are thinking harder and longer about this now and will hopefully have a lengthier update on our thinking to share in the next week.

When the METR report came out, he tweeted: "Ok so METR confirms it..."

## Navigating this:

### Are we in triage mode?

In We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety, Miles Brundage argues:

“At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)

(This reading was previously part of the AISF governance course. I was sad to see it go)

Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. Miles wrote this post in February of this year (2026), I dig more into where he might have been coming from in my full notes on his article, but I’m skipping that here as the discourse has moved on from where it was back in February.

I’ll now share some counter-perspectives (keep in mind that some of these takes were written a while back).

Firstly, Richard Ngo worries that the AI safety community is overly focused on short-timelines:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

Eliezer Yudkowsky would undoubtedly be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive.

- “But isn’t this obvious!?” — he is making the point that people often quote a year named by an expert without realising how broad their timelines actually are.
- I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I’d be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions).
- It would be interesting to know whether their forecasts have narrowed since then given that we know a lot more now than we did at the time.

Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby:

I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).

Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “radical optionality” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course). Of course, one must ask, are we still in the regime where radical optionality makes sense or are we past that now.

Specific policies:

What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion? discusses the possibility of RSI and potential policy interventions:

A big part of what makes this paper notable is its author list: “Alan Chan, Christoph Winter, Andrew Barto, Jakub Pachocki, Geoffrey Hinton, Eric Horvitz, Yoshua Bengio, Dawn Song, Jack Clark, Hilary Greaves, Anton Korinek, Samuel Hammond, Thore Graepel, Ben Bariach, Philip H. S. Torr, Sheila A. McIlraith, Jeff Clune, Sam Manning, Girish Sastry, Tom Davidson, Daniel Eth, Sören Mindermann” I suspect they’re hoping that all signing onto this paper together will make this issue credible to policy makers.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.
