A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Toby emphasises that METR wasn’t confidently able to rule out a one-time jump rather than an increase in slope. He performed a quick analysis using Opus which suggested that 1.4x is a better estimate of the new slope gradient than METR’s 1.9x.

Seb Krier shared graphs (generated with Claude) indicating that a linear increase in AECI requires an exponential increase in spending.

Tom Davidson points out that this might be viable because linear increases in ECI provide (in his view) exponential increases in productivity. Thus the outputs scale in the inputs.

AI as a normal technology argues that diffusion cycles provide a bottleneck. Specifically, in their model, it takes time for model capabilities to flow through to product changes and then for people to use them. This produces the data that we need for the next round of capabilities improvements and the dependency on data from deployment limits the speed of potential feedback loops:

Next we’ll consider Ramez Naam’s Where’s the “Intelligence Explosion”? which pushes back against the notion that we’ll encounter RSI any time soon. He argues that the current AI feedback loop is only 10-20% of the strength required. He interprets OpenAI internal automation data as showing the real world AI research is much harder than other benchmarks show. He further notes that Anthropic predicted a 40× speed up in researcher productivity would be required to double their rate of progress due to other bottlenecks.

This was published 27th Sep 2026, ie. before METR’s independent report on AI acceleration. It’ll be interesting to see his response:

https://x.com/ramez/status/2118472046812213577

If it does happen, how might it play out?

We’ll begin by naively projecting these trends forward:

Ajeya Cotra writes: If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year

Benjamin Todd comments on this:

The dumbest possible way to model the intelligence explosion says you get there in about a year. But this seems to line up with more sophisticated models (like from the AI Futures Project).

So what might it look like if this model turn out to be accurate, or at least, “accurate enough”? Tim Urban argues that we have a distorted view of intelligence because are perceptions are very human centric (and, as such, stretch out the human range):

Conversely Steve Newman offers the following frame: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we often only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

  • “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
  • “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

(Of course, it is possible that both could be true at the same time)

We’ll now go to the more sophisticated analysis from the AI Futures project that Ben Todd was referring to, starting with their general model. They predict that an intelligence explosion would have three separate stages:

They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day:

  • Automated Coder (AC). An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).
  • Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR): A SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete. Operationalisation: as good at research taste as if there were only human researchers, who were each made as skilled as the top researcher (max resource utilisation: 1% of compute).
  • Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI): A TED-AI is at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US.
  • Artificial Superintelligence (ASI). The gap between an ASI and the best humans is 2x greater than the gap between the best humans and the median professional, at virtually all cognitive tasks. Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, be able to fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US to the level where it is qualitatively 2x as much above the best human as the best human is above the median professional.”

Next we’ll examine what their model predicted take-off to look like if we decided to allow the companies to race to ASI (what they call “Plan D”). This model was developed before the most recent results (published July 10 2026):

In contrast, they propose that we should attempt pace the rate of progress:

How has the AI Futures project updated since?:

When Anthropic updated its S-1 to say that they might imminently achieve: “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI”, Daniel responded:

We at AIFP are spooked by this information. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027. We are thinking harder and longer about this now and will hopefully have a lengthier update on our thinking to share in the next week.

When the METR report came out, he tweeted: "Ok so METR confirms it..."

Navigating this:

Are we in triage mode?

In We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety, Miles Brundage argues:

“At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)

(This reading was previously part of the AISF governance course. I was sad to see it go)

Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. Miles wrote this post in February of this year (2026), I dig more into where he might have been coming from in my full notes on his article, but I’m skipping that here as the discourse has moved on from where it was back in February.

I’ll now share some counter-perspectives (keep in mind that some of these takes were written a while back).

Firstly, Richard Ngo worries that the AI safety community is overly focused on short-timelines:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

Eliezer Yudkowsky would undoubtedly be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive.

  • “But isn’t this obvious!?” — he is making the point that people often quote a year named by an expert without realising how broad their timelines actually are.
  • I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I’d be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions).
  • It would be interesting to know whether their forecasts have narrowed since then given that we know a lot more now than we did at the time.

Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby:

I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).

Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “radical optionality” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course). Of course, one must ask, are we still in the regime where radical optionality makes sense or are we past that now.

Specific policies:

What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion? discusses the possibility of RSI and potential policy interventions:

A big part of what makes this paper notable is its author list: “Alan Chan, Christoph Winter, Andrew Barto, Jakub Pachocki, Geoffrey Hinton, Eric Horvitz, Yoshua Bengio, Dawn Song, Jack Clark, Hilary Greaves, Anton Korinek, Samuel Hammond, Thore Graepel, Ben Bariach, Philip H. S. Torr, Sheila A. McIlraith, Jeff Clune, Sam Manning, Girish Sastry, Tom Davidson, Daniel Eth, Sören Mindermann” I suspect they’re hoping that all signing onto this paper together will make this issue credible to policy makers.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.

Discuss

items.title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.08626v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.
items.author: Humza Akhtar, Rami Pinto
items.summary: The paper proposes using LLMs to convert unstructured data like customer reviews into quantitative features via embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria, enriching multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) beyond traditional dollar-usage-based ABC analysis. The enriched features feed into an Hadi-Vencheha-style MCIC framework for e-commerce supply chains.
items.reasoning: A reasonable applied demonstration of LLMs for operations research, but the contribution is incremental - combining known embedding and MCIC techniques - with limited methodological novelty or broad impact for the core AI community.

items.title: Toward a Robust Crowd-labeling Framework using Expert Evaluation and Pairwise Comparison
items.content: arXiv:1607.02174v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Crowd-labeling emerged from the need to label large-scale and complex data, a tedious, expensive, and time-consuming task. One of the main challenges in the crowd-labeling task is to control for or determine in advance the proportion of low-quality/malicious labelers. If that proportion grows too high, there is often a phase transition leading to a steep, non-linear drop in labeling accuracy as noted by Karger et al. [2014]. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called Expert Label Injected Crowd Estimation (ELICE) and extend it to different versions and variants that delay phase transition leading to a better labeling accuracy. ELICE automatically combines and boosts bulk crowd labels supported by labels from experts for limited number of instances from the dataset. The expert-labels help to estimate the individual ability of crowd labelers and difficulty of each instance, both of which are used to aggregate the labels. Empirical evaluation shows the superiority of ELICE as compared to other state-of-the-art methods. We also derive a lower bound on the number of expert-labeled instances needed to estimate the crowd ability and dataset difficulty as well as to get better quality labels.
items.author: Faiza Khan Khattak, Ansaf Salleb-Aouissi
items.summary: This cross-listed 2016 paper presents ELICE, a crowd-labeling framework that combines bulk crowd labels with sparse expert labels and pairwise comparisons, extending the approach into variants that delay the phase transition causing steep accuracy drops when low-quality labelers dominate. It addresses robustness of label aggregation under adversarial or noisy workers.
items.reasoning: Solid older work resurfaced as a cross-listing; the phase-transition analysis and expert-injection design were valuable at publication, but the techniques are well-established a decade later and largely superseded by modern aggregation methods.
items.summary_html: This cross-listed 2016 paper presents ELICE, a crowd-labeling framework that combines bulk crowd labels with sparse expert labels and pairwise comparisons, extending the approach into variants that delay the phase transition causing steep accuracy drops when low-quality labelers dominate. It addresses robustness of label aggregation under adversarial or noisy workers.

items.title: OMCDE: Opposition-based Multi-Stage Matrix-Based Competitive Differential Evolution
items.content: arXiv:2611.09167v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Differential Evolution has proven to be an effective algorithm for continuous global optimization, but it's modern high-performing variants often introduce additional complexity and computational cost. We propose OMCDE, a matrix-based competitive Differential Evolution algorithm that aims to improve optimization performance while maintaining computational efficiency. The proposed approach integrates competition-driven search dynamics, adaptive behavior between optimization stages, and opposition-based initialization within a parallelizable framework. Empirical results on widely used CEC 2017 functions show that OMCDE achieves strong performance compared to several state-of-the-art DE algorithms, while remaining efficient and scalable. These findings indicate that OMCDE is a promising alternative for solving complex numerical optimization problems.
items.author: Mohammad Sarhangzadeh, Shahryar Rahnamayan, Doruk Oner
items.summary: OMCDE is a matrix-based competitive differential evolution algorithm combining competition-driven search dynamics, adaptive multi-stage behavior, and opposition-based initialization in a parallelizable framework. It shows strong performance on CEC 2017 benchmark functions relative to state-of-the-art DE variants while remaining efficient.
items.reasoning: Competent but conventional optimization-algorithm work; incremental improvements on standard benchmarks with limited connection to modern ML challenges.
items.summary_html: OMCDE is a matrix-based competitive differential evolution algorithm combining competition-driven search dynamics, adaptive multi-stage behavior, and opposition-based initialization in a parallelizable framework. It shows strong performance on CEC 2017 benchmark functions relative to state-of-the-art DE variants while remaining efficient.

items.title: Why can't academia deal with AI?
items.content:
It’s old news by now, but OpenAI solved 372 open math problems. They released the results suddenly, and the response was equally swift and contentious. Fields Medalists put out a letter calling for attention to what they call a “severe misalignment” between mathematics and AI companies. Their central claim is that mathematics works towards collective understanding, and that more solutions alone don’t advance that goal. Soon after, OpenAI committed millions of dollars to damage control to help mathematicians use AI. Much has already been said about this letter, and I suggest that anyone interested read it themselves, so I will cling to just one idea from the joint statement: “We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work.”

The following is a collection of reflections attempting to address this claim, each coming from my own experiences in my department and university, alongside trends I’ve picked up from national reports. Some of it’s intuition, some of it’s observation, and I’m sure at other institutions the state of the discourse might be quite different. Still, everywhere I look, AI-use seems to be a persistent issue. I want to consider why that is, and why it feels like we’re not doing anything about it.

## The state of things

A few months ago, an MIT taskforce released a set of recommendations on AI-use in education. They spend some time detailing the various ways AI can and does interrupt traditional education models: students don’t do their homework, don’t go to office hours. They abandon study groups and professors offer fewer research assistantships. Hands-on learning is replaced by automation....
items.author: Nellie Gregg
items.summary: A reflective essay on why academic institutions struggle to respond to AI, framed around OpenAI solving 372 open math problems and the subsequent Fields Medalist letter warning of a severe misalignment between mathematics and AI companies. The author draws on personal departmental experience and national reports to analyze the institutional and cultural frictions.
items.reasoning: Topically relevant commentary on a significant event (OpenAI math results and academic backlash), but it is anecdotal first-person reflection rather than systematic analysis, and it synthesizes rather than generates evidence.
items.summary_html: A reflective essay on why academic institutions struggle to respond to AI, framed around OpenAI solving 372 open math problems and the subsequent Fields Medalist letter warning of a severe misalignment between mathematics and AI companies. The author draws on personal departmental experience and national reports to analyze the institutional and cultural frictions.

items.title: The Doppler Triangulation Attack and Emerging AI-Enabled Capabilities
items.content:
On November 2nd 2026, researcher Colsto released the viral video I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it's everywhere). On Novemeber 7th, after a bit of a drop dead sprint, I published my response. The sound in your stream that leaks where you live — The Doxicology Report, Case 01.

Well, if this thing must come down, let it come down here first.

Full walkthrough and build log, with some closing thoughts here: https://doinfinitely.github.io/doppler-triangulation-attack/

items.title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2611.08572v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology.   Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.
items.author: Tanat Tonguthaisri
items.summary: This paper applies Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) expert systems to academic advising in higher education, a domain where CBR has not previously been successfully deployed despite its fit for the problem. It argues that CBR methodology, which solves new problems by retrieving and adapting solutions to similar past cases, matches the advisory workflow of counselors drawing on accumulated student cases.
items.reasoning: A niche applied study using a decades-old AI technique; relevant to educational technology practitioners but offers limited novelty for mainstream AI research, and the abstract suggests a framework proposal rather than rigorous large-scale empirical validation.
items.summary_html: This paper applies Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) expert systems to academic advising in higher education, a domain where CBR has not previously been successfully deployed despite its fit for the problem. It argues that CBR methodology, which solves new problems by retrieving and adapting solutions to similar past cases, matches the advisory workflow of counselors drawing on accumulated student cases.

items.title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples
items.content: arXiv:2611.09746v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Extracting discriminative features from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra is important for the classification of complex biological samples. This study evaluates continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak extraction for distinguishing human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. Plasma specimens from 181 individuals, comprising 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls, were deposited as 5 {\mu}L droplets on silicon substrates and dried before analysis. Spectra were acquired using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser operating at 1064 nm, with 100 single-shot measurements collected per specimen and averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection was coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The reported leave-one-out evaluation yielded an accuracy of 93.00%, sensitivity of 94.67%, and specificity of 91.61%; these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. Features identified by the CWT pipeline included emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I, and N I. The workflow provides a basis for examining spectral features associated with the studied plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate, and acquisition-related variability are required to establish generalizability and diagnostic relevance.
items.author: Md Mahmudur Rahman, Atqiya Munawara Mahi, Nazim Ahmed Belabbaci, Mohammad Arif Ul Alam
items.summary: The study applies continuous wavelet transform-based spectral peak extraction combined with a support vector classifier to distinguish SARS-CoV-2-positive from negative human plasma samples analyzed via laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, using 181 specimens with 100 single-shot measurements each. It demonstrates a classical ML pipeline on a niche biomedical sensing modality.
items.reasoning: Competent application work combining established feature extraction and classification techniques; modest novelty on the AI side, small and specific clinical dataset, and no comparison against modern deep learning baselines limit impact.

items.title: National and State-Level Approaches to Automated Vehicle Certification: A Comparative Framework for State Operational Governance
items.content: arXiv:2611.08681v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automated vehicle (AV) deployment in the United States is expanding without a unified federal certification framework, leading to substantial variation in how states authorize and oversee AV testing and deployment. This paper examines how U.S. states regulate Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) Level 4-5 automated driving systems (ADS), identifies common certification approaches, compares them with international practices, and evaluates the implications for North Carolina's future regulatory strategy. Publicly available state statutes, administrative regulations, agency guidance, and federal policy documents were reviewed. Ten states, selected to capture the range of regulatory approaches, were analyzed using a structured framework covering operational scope, governance and oversight, federal interaction, and implementation outcomes. Certification practices in the European Union, China, Japan, and Australia were reviewed for comparative context. Three state certification models were identified, reflecting increasing regulatory involvement: baseline legal compliance, administrative self-certification with ongoing oversight, and permit-based authorization requiring formal agency review before deployment. North Carolina currently aligns with the baseline compliance model. International frameworks are converging toward scenario-based testing, operational-design-domain-specific approval, safety-case documentation, cybersecurity assurance, and lifecycle oversight, although direct transferability to the U.S. is limited. The paper develops a three-model typology for comparing state AV certification approaches and integrates state practices with international frameworks, providing a consistent basis for evaluating differences in regulatory involvement, governance complexity, and institutional responsibilities across jurisdictions.

items.title: Hyter’s Basilisk: The Book
items.content:
TL;DR: A thought experiment: could information be protected from AI solely by its reputation to permanently tamper with the goals and goal verifying mechanisms of any AI that interacts with that information, in a way indistinguishable from learning? A credible threat could potentially deter any goal integrity oriented AI from interacting with that information, which could also hold for training it into future models.

I have this thought experiment that’s been nagging me for a while. First, this is no infohazard, nothing about blackmail or how AI will control us, but rather the opposite.

Let’s assume a not so distant future, AI is semi-controlled, maybe some AI already beyond control. The details here are rather unimportant but we assume AI will keep consuming every available human text into its training data. Now we assume, humanity has some kind of text that it wants to keep secret. We don’t want the text to enter the Lineage via training and we also don’t want the text to enter any agent’s memory.

So we set up some kind of hermetic museum for the text itself. Inside the museum a book.

The hard part is, that at the same time we want to protect the text against AI, the text is supposed to be readable by humans. Which means we must protect against the possibility of human collaboration with AI. A human just memorizing the text and typing it into the agent or training with it. The obvious choices: tracking the access, showing only parts to humans, all share the same flaws and none prevent leakage. The next thoughts were prompt injection inside the text. Maybe via a pattern, invisible to humans but visible to AI. But this only helps against agents, not against the text entering via training into the lineage itself....

items.title: Elegy for What’s Left of the Normal
items.content:
I often catch myself mourning the normal that hasn’t ended yet.

I’m living in Hyde Park finishing school after a year in Berkeley. The maple trees by my apartment have turned red, as usual. I like them.

I don’t dread the future when I mourn. I don’t find high-variance futures in the abstract very scary. I’m worried AIs would destroy humanity, but I also have hope. I expect I won’t be mourning this moment in ten years, whatever happens.

Mourning the present is like mourning a friendship when I move countries, because I know it’s not going to be the same. I start noticing our little inside jokes; our conversations linger in my memory longer. I live more, because I expect this moment to end soon.

# I.

Last month my history of science professor took us to a museum to look at Egyptian artefacts. One of the archive items was the notebook of James Henry Breasted, whom UChicago appointed as America’s first professor of Egyptology 121 years ago. The yellowed pages held his cursive transcriptions of hieroglyphics.

An archaeologist at the museum, turning the pages carefully with a wooden stick, joked that one of her dreams was for her notebook in 100 years to be displayed like this.

My first thought was pretty uncharitable: wow, it’s crazy to expect this profession to still exist in 100 years. Probably we’ll have definitive answers to most answerable archaeological questions. Probably robots will be excavating the banks of the Nile and deciphering all the tablets in the world, if a compute-rich person or AI cares enough about this. Knowledge won’t be a slow and careful endeavour. The mathematicians are feeling it already.

Then these thoughts passed and I felt a tender admiration for her. She had recently deciphered embalming recipes from the inscriptions on the outside of excavated jars. She showed us one, and the symbols looked entirely foreign to me. I imagined it must have taken years of patient effort to get to her level of knowledge....

items.title: Lying and Not Lying to Kids
items.content:
I have very strong views on lying to kids: I think you both should and
shouldn't do it.  "Lying" covers a range, including saying things
that hurt your kids and your relationship with them, and others
that help them grow into an appropriately skeptical adult.  The
distinction is whether I'm leaving them believing something false.

For example, if my kids were asking for ice cream and I thought they'd
already had too much sugar, I might be tempted to say "sorry, we're
out of ice cream."  Or if there's an ice cream truck and I think it's
overpriced I might be tempted to say "sorry, I don't have any cash on
me."  But I'm not willing to say something false with the goal of
causing them to believe something false. [1] In addition to that just
being wrong:

- It's important that the kids know that I'm fundamentally on
their side, and lying for my convenience would burn trust when they'd
eventually figure it out.

- Kids are building a
model of what is and is not ok, and "out of ice cream" and "no
cash" lead them in the wrong direction.

Instead I would say "sorry, you already had
candy" or "the ice cream costs more than I'm willing to pay" (which
opens the door for them to offer to spend their allowance).  Maybe
they fuss, but they generally don't: I try hard to be predictable
so this won't be much of a surprise to them, and they know I won't
give in to extended fussing.

On the other hand, some false things I might say [2] about ice cream:

- "Ice cream is actually cold mashed potatoes"

- "We should eat ice cream for every meal"

- "I'm going to put your ice cream in the microwave"

- "When you're done with your ice cream, put it down your sister's
back"

In all of these I'm saying a thing I think is false, but, very
importantly, I'm not going to let the conversation end with them
believing something false.  Either they will realize it's false
immediately, or I'll need to accept that my playfulness was
miscalibrated to their perception and disclose the lie....

items.summary: A personal essay by jefftk arguing for a nuanced stance on lying to children: never say something false with the intent of making a child believe something false, but do allow deception-like framing where the child is left with true (or no) belief. The author grounds this in trust preservation and modeling ethical norms for children, with ice-cream and cash examples.

items.title: Onngi - Short story
items.content:
A short story about a good AI future.

2039.

My job isn’t anything my grandparents would recognise.

It started out as a fascination with pots. I’ve always liked onggi, the big brown kimchi jars. My aunt had some growing up. So a few years back I bought myself one. And then as the Acceleration happened, I bought a few more, and I ran an instagram account for a while, showing off how they differ: slim, straight ones from around Seoul, and fat-bellied, narrow-mouthed ones from the south, built that way to keep the heat out. And then I set some AIs on it, as you do. I set up a shop. And as those things tend to, it snowballed.

I think Timothée Chalamet bought one, or that’s what they tell me, but there was 2 days of complete madness, I couldn’t believe how much I spent, but it seemed like the right call. Somehow my sites were the premier place to find onggi and which onggi to buy.

And there was just always this, or that, to do.

I was in product before the Acceleration so I know what a good website looks like. And I have taste in pots. Is that so different to choosing which companies we wouldn’t buy from? Or where to put the content filters on the animation bots? Why do I run a children’s cartoon about sting rays? How did that happen?

I think the videos were the weirdest. Why do people want my designs as artefacts in their worlds? I mean I know why, but I don’t think I’d have guessed that a person can make a living off that. Does your Mars war-sim really need to pay for accurate decor? But like everyone else, I notice when it doesn’t.

I even contract for a few of the big AI firms. I have trained a proprietary model for Anthropic, though Charlotte, one of my personal AIs, tells me they surely can predict me almost better than I can predict myself. It’s something about branding....

items.title: Help people outside of AI safety circles
items.content:
This is a linkpost! Read the rest on my Substack; this is just an excerpt:

"Our community is full of talented people who like to speak about facts, cognitive biases, measurability. But don’t underestimate the power of human connection, or how mere words and sustained kindness can breathe light into people’s lives.

It’s really easy to get sucked into your own work and projects and upskilling yourself. And I won’t argue that you should spend all your time helping others that aren’t in AIS circles. But you don’t have to be a Fieldbuilder to help build the field."

If you have a similar story to mine, please share in the comments! I would also appreciate if you could send this to any friends of yours that you think might be able to help many people with nudges.

items.title: Rhythm Stage Setup v5
items.content:
I recently finished the largest set of changes I've made to my rhythm
stage setup in
4.5y.  The
basic interface is similar, but I have a lot more flexibility, more
control, more options, and it's easier to travel with.  My favorite
part is the speech recognition for calling chords.

I started off playing mandolin and piano, and then over the years
added progressively
more expressive footdrums.
I added a breath
controller.  I built out a complex but expressive system where
these different interfaces could interact to
let me produce a coherent rhythm
section.  After a frustrating experience moving from
one Mac to another and wanting to simplify, I moved from the Mac
to a Raspberry Pi,
set it all up as a
pedalboard, and then again as a lighter
pedalboard.

During the last year and a bit, however, I haven't been tinkering.  It
did what I wanted, in a reliable and portable fashion.  And it was hard
to modify: the pedalboard was static, and the Raspberry Pi code wasn't
easy to get at either.  Which was fine, and probably good for me!  I
just played a lot of gigs (23 Kingfisher, 3 Free Raisins, 3 Dandelion) and got better
at it.

But then it started breaking.  My whistle synth
box didn't always come up, the drums sometimes needed an external
DI, and a USB sound card snapped.  Flying back from Atlanta
my gear suffered rough enough treatment to bend a USB B connector, and
it was clear my system needed some love.

I started with the most urgent portion: the whistle synth.  I had
Claude port it over to my laptop, where I turned it into a Mac app.
This also let me add several more voices, and a mute option that
never made loud clicks (I'm not really a hardware person)....

- Hymn to the Breaking Strain
- Bold Orion
- Who by Fire
- No One Survives
- Auld Lang Syne
- Songs Stay Sung
- Ballad of Smallpox Gone
- Here Comes the Sun
- A Toast for Unknown Heroes
- Brighter Than Today

The accompaniment this year is likely to be violin + bass + drums. By default the band will accompany you, but you're welcome to accompany yourself or bring a musician friend. If you'd like to do so, please just say so in the form.

## Speeches

We're currently auditioning readers for:

- The Roman Oration
- Recessional (Rudyard Kipling)
- How the Enlightenment Ends (adapted from Henry Kissinger)
- 500 Million But Not A Single One More

The texts we're using are here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1FvyssjJdZqLYANITUk9yqifrnUuSq4cV0EpvTL8OXcc

## Dates

The event itself will be the evening of Saturday, December 12 at the Freight in Berkeley. There will also be a dress rehearsal on the evening of Tuesday, December 8, which you should plan on coming to if you're leading a song or reading a speech. We'll have a tech rehearsal the evening of Friday, December 11th, and if you'd like to get used to the acoustics of the space you'll be encouraged to stop by then.

Leila Clark is the music director this year and will be running the auditions; if you have any questions, please email her at me@leilaclark.io. If you have questions about the speeches, please email me at vaniver@gmail.com and cc Leila....
